﴿We do not send down the angels except with truth﴾: it was read as "*ma nunazzilu*" with the *nun*, in the active voice, with God (glory be to Him) as the agent, so it is from "sending down" (*tanzil*). The meaning in this reading: God (glory be to Him) said, answering the disbelievers when they asked for the angels to come to them: "We do not send down the angels except with truth," i.e., sending them down clothed in the truth that justifies their sending down to them in what the divine wisdom and the lordly will require. What you have proposed is not something for which the sending down of angels is justified. It was also read *nunzilu* (without doubling), from *inzal* (causing to descend). It was read also *ma tanazzalu* with the *ta'* at the beginning, as an imperfect verb in the intensive form, active voice, from *tanzil*, with one of the two *ta'*s elided, i.e., *tatanazzalu* (they descend). It was also read with the *ta'* at the beginning as an imperfect verb in the passive voice. It was said that the meaning of "except with truth" is: except with the Qur'an; it was said: with the message; it was said: with punishment. (And they would not be given respite.) There is an ellipsis in the speech; the estimated meaning is: "Had We sent down the angels, they would have been hastened to punishment, and they would not have been given respite." Thus the clause mentioned is the answer to the omitted conditional clause.

Then He denounced the disbelievers' mockery of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) by their saying: ﴿O you to whom the Reminder has been sent, you are surely a madman!﴾ So He (glory be to Him) said: ﴿Indeed, We Ourselves sent down the Reminder﴾ — i.e., We Ourselves sent down that Reminder, which they denied and because of which they attributed madness to you. ﴿And indeed We are its guardians﴾ — against everything unbefitting it, such as distortion, alteration, addition, omission, and the like.

In this there is a severe warning to those who deny it and mock the Messenger of God (ﷺ). It was said that the pronoun in "its" refers to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), but the first is more suitable to the context.

Then (glory be to Him) mentioned that the custom of such disbelievers with their prophets was the same, as consolation for the Messenger of God (ﷺ). So He said: ﴿We certainly sent (messengers) before you﴾ — i.e., messengers, the word being omitted because the sending indicates it: messengers who existed before you ﴿among the sects of the former peoples﴾ — among their nations, their followers, and all their factions and groups.

Al-Farra' said: *shiya'* (sects) means the community following one another in what they agree upon. Its root is from *sha'ahu*, meaning he followed him. Its being attributed to "the former peoples" is either an attribution of a qualifier to the qualified, according to some grammarians, or an ellipsis of the qualified, according to others.

﴿No messenger came to them but they mocked him.﴾ I.e., no messenger among the messengers came to his followers except that they mocked him, as these disbelievers do with Muhammad (ﷺ). The clause ﴿but they mocked him﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, or in the nominative position as a qualifier of "messenger," or in the genitive position as a qualifier of it according to its form, not its location.

﴿Thus We let it enter into the hearts of the criminals.﴾ I.e., in the same way as We made it enter the hearts of those who mocked their messengers, We let the Reminder — i.e., the Reminder — enter into the hearts of the criminals. So the demonstrative refers to what the preceding speech indicates, namely the sending of revelation accompanied by mockery. *Al-salk* means the insertion of one thing into another, like a thread into a needle, as al-Zajjaj said. He said: the meaning is, just as We did to the criminals who mocked, We make error enter the hearts of the criminals.

The clause ﴿They do not believe in it﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ﴿We let it enter﴾, i.e., they do not believe in the Reminder that We have sent down. It is also permissible that it be a new sentence explaining what precedes it, in which case it has no grammatical position. It was also said that the pronoun in ﴿We let it enter﴾ refers to mockery, and the pronoun in ﴿They do not believe in it﴾ refers to the Reminder, but this is far-fetched. The more correct view is that both pronouns refer to the Reminder.

﴿Though the way of the former peoples has already passed.﴾ I.e., their established way, which God ordained regarding their destruction, has already passed, since they did what they did of denial and mockery.

Al-Zajjaj said: the sunna of God regarding the former peoples has passed, namely that He let disbelief and error enter their hearts.

Then God (glory be to Him) related their persistence in disbelief and their determination in denial and mockery.

Then He said: ﴿Even if We opened for them a gate into the heaven﴾, meaning for these obstinate opponents of Muhammad (ﷺ), who denied him and mocked him, ﴿a gate from the sky﴾, meaning from its known gates, and We enabled them to ascend through it, ﴿and they continued to ascend through it﴾, meaning through that gate, ﴿ascending﴾, meaning climbing, whether by means of an instrument or without one, until they witnessed what is in the heaven of the wonders of the malakut (the unseen dominion of God), which no denier could deny and no obstinate person could oppose upon seeing it. It has also been said that the pronoun in ﴿they continued﴾ refers to the angels, meaning that the angels continued to ascend through that gate while the unbelievers watched them and observed their ascent through that gate. ﴿They would surely say﴾, meaning the unbelievers, because of the extremity of their obstinacy and the increase of their defiance: ﴿Our eyes have only been intoxicated.﴾ Ibn Kathir read ﴿سُكِرَتْ﴾ (sukirat) with light emphasis, while the rest read it with the doubled letter (sukkirat). It is from the intoxication of drink, or from sakr, which means blocking the senses, as one says sakara al-nahr (he dammed the river) when he dams it and holds it back from flowing. The second meaning was preferred on the basis of the light reading.

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: ﴿سُكِّرَتْ﴾ means "it was covered and veiled." From this is the verse of the poet:

*And a sun rose over them, with a helmet of mail,*
*and the eye of the heat-haze began to be blocked.*

This is also the view of Abu 'Ubayd and Abu 'Ubayda. It is also narrated from Abu 'Amr that it is from the intoxication of drink, meaning that what covers their sight overtook them as intoxication overtakes the drunkard, covering his intellect. It has also been said that the meaning of ﴿سُكِّرَتْ﴾ is "held back," as already mentioned. From this is the verse of Aws ibn Hajar:

*So I remained awake through a night of watching,*
*and it was neither clear nor blocked.*

Al-Nahhas said: these views are close in meaning.

﴿Rather, we are a people who have been bewitched﴾: they turned away from their statement "our eyes have been intoxicated," and then claimed that they were bewitched, meaning that Muhammad (ﷺ) had bewitched them.

In this there is an explanation of their great obstinacy, which nothing whatsoever can turn them away from. When they see a sign that obliges them to believe in God, His angels, His books and His messengers, they attribute to their eyes that their perception of it is not real, due to an intoxicating impediment, or they claim that their intellects have been bewitched, so their perception has become unsound. Whoever has reached this degree of stubbornness, admonition will not benefit him, and he will not be guided by any sign.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid concerning God's words ﴿These are the verses of the Book﴾ that he said: "the Torah and the Gospel."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated concerning ﴿These are the verses of the Book﴾ that he said: "the books that came before the Qur'an." Concerning ﴿and a clear Qur'an﴾ he said: "Clear, by God, its guidance, its rectitude and its good."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud and some of the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning God's words ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims﴾, that he said: "The polytheists wished on the Day of Badr, when their necks were struck and they were presented to the Fire, that they had been believers in Muhammad (ﷺ)."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Mas'ud concerning the verse that he said: "This is about the people of Hell when they see them coming out of the Fire."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Hannad ibn al-Sari in al-Zuhd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th wa al-Nushur narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "God continues to intercede, and to admit, and to intercede, and to show mercy, until He says: whoever was a Muslim, let him enter Paradise. That is His words: ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims﴾."

Ibn al-Mubarak in al-Zuhd, Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Anas that they discussed this verse, ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims﴾, and they said: "This is when God gathers the people of sins, from among the Muslims and the polytheists, into the Fire, and the polytheists say: what your worship benefited you is nothing. Then God becomes angry on their behalf and brings them out by His grace and mercy."

al-Tabarani in al-Awsat and Ibn Mardawayh narrated with a chain, which al-Suyuti said is sahih, from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Some people of my community will be punished for their sins and will remain in the Fire as long as God wills. Then the people of polytheism will reproach them, saying: We do not see that what you believed in benefited you. So no one who affirms God's oneness will remain but God will bring him out of the Fire." Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited: ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims﴾.

Ibn Abi 'Asim in al-Sunna, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar.

Ishaq ibn Rahawayh, Ibn Hibban, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar as well.

Hannad ibn al-Sari, al-Tabarani in al-Awsat and Abu Nu'aym narrated from Anas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar also.

There are hadiths on the matter that specify the cause of the revelation of this verse.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Zayd concerning God's words ﴿Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves﴾, the verse, that he said: "These are the disbelievers."

He also narrated from Abu Malik concerning God's words, ﴿Leave them﴾, that he said: "Let them alone."

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Zuhri concerning God's words ﴿No nation precedes its term, nor do they delay﴾, that he said: "We hold that when its term arrives, it is not delayed an hour nor advanced. As for what has not yet reached its term, God delays whom He wills and advances whom He wills."

I say: this statement of al-Zuhri has no substance and no benefit in it.

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Dahhak concerning God's words ﴿O you to whom the Reminder has been sent﴾, that he said: "The Qur'an."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid concerning God's words ﴿We do not send down the angels except with truth﴾, that he said: "With the message and the punishment."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi concerning God's words ﴿And they would not have been reprieved﴾, that he said: "And they would not, even if the angels descended, have been reprieved from being punished."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid concerning ﴿And indeed We are its guardians﴾, that he said: "With Us."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning God's words ﴿among the sects of the former peoples﴾, that he said: "the nations of the former peoples."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Anas concerning God's words ﴿Thus We insert it into the hearts of the criminals﴾, that he said: "Polytheism, We insert it into the hearts of the polytheists."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatada something similar.

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from al-Hasan something similar also.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatada concerning ﴿And the example of the former peoples has already passed﴾, that he said: "the events of God concerning those among the nations who passed away."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Jurayj concerning God's words ﴿and they continued to ascend through it﴾, that Ibn Jurayj said: Ibn 'Abbas said: "The angels continued to ascend, and they looked at them, and said: ﴿Our eyes have only been intoxicated﴾." He said: "It is the Quraysh who say it."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated concerning the verse, also from Ibn 'Abbas, that he said: "If We opened for them a gate from the gates of heaven, and the angels continued to ascend through it, going and coming in disagreement about it, the people of polytheism would say: our sight has only been taken away and confused for us, and we have only been bewitched."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid concerning ﴿Our eyes have been intoxicated﴾ that he said: "They have been blocked."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatada something similar, and said: "Whoever reads ﴿سُكِرَتْ﴾ with the light emphasis, he means ﴿سُحِرَتْ﴾ (suhirat), 'bewitched'."

Its classification as Meccan is agreed upon, as al-Qurtubi said.

Al-Nahhas in his *Nasikh* (on abrogation, *naskh*) and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Surat al-Hijr was revealed in Mecca."

Ibn Mardawayh also narrated from Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr something similar.

﴿Alif. Lam. Ra. These are the verses of the Book and a clear Qur'an.﴾ ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims.﴾ ﴿Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves, and let hope distract them. They will soon know.﴾ ﴿We never destroyed a town without its having a known decreed term.﴾ ﴿No nation can hasten its term, nor can it delay it.﴾ ﴿They say: "O you to whom the Reminder has been sent, you are surely a madman!"﴾ ﴿"Why do you not bring us angels, if you are among the truthful?"﴾ ﴿We do not send down the angels except with truth, and then they would not be given respite.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We Ourselves sent down the Reminder, and indeed We are its guardians.﴾ ﴿We certainly sent (messengers) before you among the sects of the former peoples.﴾ ﴿No messenger came to them but they mocked him.﴾ ﴿Thus We let it enter into the hearts of the criminals.﴾ ﴿They do not believe in it, though the way of the former peoples has already passed.﴾ ﴿Even if We opened for them a gate in the sky and they kept ascending through it,﴾ ﴿they would say, "Our eyes have only been dazzled; rather, we are a people bewitched."﴾

Regarding His words ﴿Alif Lam Ra﴾: the discussion of it has already been given in full in its proper place. The demonstrative in ﴿These are the verses﴾ refers to what the surah contains of verses. The definiteness in "the Book" is said to be generic (*li-l-jins*), meaning the category of previous scriptures. It was also said that it refers to the Qur'an; the mention of "the Qur'an" after "the Book" does not undermine this, since it has been said that He combined the two names for it. It was also said that "the Book" means this surah itself. The indefiniteness of "a Qur'an" is for magnification, i.e., the complete Qur'an.

﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims.﴾ Nafi' and Asim read the *ba'* of *rubama* with a light (single) pronunciation, while the rest read it with emphasis (doubled). Both are dialects. Abu Hatim said: "The people of the Hijaz pronounce it lightly," and from this is the poet's verse:

*Rubba darbatin bi-saifin saqilin / bayna Busra wa-ta'natin najla'*
(Many a blow with a polished sword between Busra and a wide-gaping spear-thrust.)

The Tamim and Rabi'a tribes pronounce it with emphasis. The *ta'* (feminine) may be added to it, and its original use is for the few, though it may also be used for the many. The Kufans said: the meaning is that the disbelievers will wish, at many times, that they had been Muslims. From this is the poet's verse:

*Rubba rafdin harraqtahu dhalika al-yawma / wa-asra min ma'shari aqyali*
(How many a gift you poured out that day, and captives from a folk of chieftains.)

It was also said that *rubba* here is for paucity, because they wished for this at some times and not at all times, being occupied with the punishment. It is said that *ma* here is attached to *rubba* to prepare it to enter upon a verb. It was also said that it is an indefinite noun meaning "a thing." *Rubba* enters here upon the future, although it only enters upon the past, because what is awaited in His report (glory be to Him) is like what has occurred and is certain; it is as if it were said: "Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims," i.e., submitting to His judgment, humbly accepting it, among its people.

This wishing from them occurs at the time of their death or on the Day of Resurrection. The meaning is that when the matter became clear to them, and the falsity of what they had been upon of disbelief became evident, and that religion before God (glory be to Him) is Islam, with no religion other than it, this wishing arose in them, which neither fattens nor satisfies hunger. Rather, it is merely regret, remorse, and self-reproach over what they neglected regarding God's right. It was said that this wishing from them occurs upon witnessing their state and the state of the Muslims. It was also said that it occurs when the sinners among the monotheists come out of the Fire. The apparent meaning is that this wishing is constantly present in them at every moment after the matter has been revealed to them.

﴿Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves﴾: this is a threat to them, i.e., leave them to what you are engaged in of commanding and forbidding them. They will never mend their ways, nor leave falsehood, nor enter into truth. Rather, let them be with what they are occupied with: eating and enjoying the flower of this world. They are like cattle, which concern themselves only with that and occupy themselves with nothing else. The meaning is: leave them to what they are upon of occupation with eating and the like, with the goods of this world, and with hope distracting them from following you. "They will soon know" the outcome of their affair and the evil of their deeds.

In this there is a threat and a rebuke of an immeasurable measure (p-٧٥٦). It is said: *alhahu kadha*, i.e., he occupied him; *lahā 'ani al-shay'i yalhu*, i.e., he was distracted from the thing. The meaning is: hope occupied them away from following the truth. They continued in empty hopes and false wishes until the morning became clear to the one who has two eyes, the matter was uncovered, and they saw the punishment on the Day of Resurrection. At that time they will taste the evil consequence of what they did.

The three verbs are jussive because they are the answer to the imperative. This verse is abrogated (*mansukha*) by the verse of the sword.

﴿We never destroyed a town without its having a known decreed term.﴾ I.e., We never destroyed any town among the towns with any kind of punishment, ﴿except that﴾ — for that town there is a *kitab*, i.e., a fixed term that it cannot precede or delay, known, not unknown or forgotten. Thus, it is inconceivable that it could deviate from it in any way. The clause "for it is a Book" is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring to "town." Although it is indefinite, it has taken the status of a qualified noun because of the generality it carries. The *waw* distinguishes whether this clause is a circumstantial clause or a qualifier, for it specifies it as circumstantial, as in your saying: "my state is a man with a sword on his shoulder." It was also said that the clause is a qualifier of "town," and the *waw* serves to emphasize the adhesion between the qualifier and the qualified.

﴿No nation can hasten its term.﴾ I.e., no nation among the nations can precede its term, which has been set for it and written in the Preserved Tablet (*al-Lawh al-Mahfuz*). The meaning is that its destruction does not come before its term arrives. ﴿Nor can they delay it.﴾ I.e., they cannot be late in relation to it, so that their destruction comes after the appointed term has passed. The use of the verb in the masculine plural form is for the sake of meaning, with predominance, and for the sake of the rhyme endings; therefore the prepositional phrase has been omitted. The clause explains what precedes it, as if it were said: this respite should not deceive the wise, for every nation has a specific time for the descent of punishment, which neither precedes nor follows.

The explanation of "term" (*ajal*) has already been given at the beginning of Surat al-An'am.

Then, when He had finished with the threat against the disbelievers, He began to explain some of their obstinacy in disbelief and their persistence in error, together with its inclusion of a demonstration of their disbelief in the one to whom the Book was revealed, after demonstrating their disbelief in the Book. So He said: ﴿They say: "O you to whom the Reminder has been sent!"﴾ I.e., the disbelievers of Mecca said, addressing the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and mocking him, since they affirmed for him the sending down of the Reminder while in reality they denied it most strongly and rejected it most emphatically. Or they meant by ﴿O you to whom the Reminder has been sent﴾ — according to his claim and in accordance with what he asserts — ﴿you are surely a madman!﴾ I.e., because of this claim you make, that you are a messenger of God commanded to convey His rulings, you are surely mad, for no one who was sane would claim such a great claim in their view. Their saying this to Muhammad (ﷺ) is like the saying of Pharaoh: ﴿Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is surely mad﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:27].

﴿Why do you not bring us angels﴾: *law ma* is a particle of urging, composed of *law*, which conveys wishing, and the extra *ma*. Thus the whole conveys urging to the action into which it enters. The meaning is: "Why do you not bring us angels, so that they may bear witness to your truthfulness, if you are among the truthful?"

Al-Farra' said: the *mim* in *lawma* is a substitute for the *lam* in *lawla*. Al-Kisa'i said: *lawla* and *lawma* are the same in statement and in question. Al-Nahhas said: *lawma*, *lawla*, and *halla* are one and the same. It was also said: the meaning is "Why do you not bring us angels, so that they would punish us for our denial of you?"

﴿We do not send down the angels except with truth﴾: it was read as "*ma nunazzilu*" with the *nun*, in the active voice, with God (glory be to Him) as the agent, so it is from "sending down" (*tanzil*). The meaning in this reading: God (glory be to Him) said, answering the disbelievers when they asked for the angels to come to them: "We do not send down the angels except with truth," i.e., sending them down clothed in the truth that justifies their sending down to them in what the divine wisdom and the lordly will require. What you have proposed is not something for which the sending down of angels is justified. It was also read *nunzilu* (without doubling), from *inzal* (causing to descend). It was read also *ma tanazzalu* with the *ta'* at the beginning, as an imperfect verb in the intensive form, active voice, from *tanzil*, with one of the two *ta'*s elided, i.e., *tatanazzalu* (they descend). It was also read with the *ta'* at the beginning as an imperfect verb in the passive voice. It was said that the meaning of "except with truth" is: except with the Qur'an; it was said: with the message; it was said: with punishment. (And they would not be given respite.) There is an ellipsis in the speech; the estimated meaning is: "Had We sent down the angels, they would have been hastened to punishment, and they would not have been given respite." Thus the clause mentioned is the answer to the omitted conditional clause.

Then He denounced the disbelievers' mockery of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) by their saying: ﴿O you to whom the Reminder has been sent, you are surely a madman!﴾ So He (glory be to Him) said: ﴿Indeed, We Ourselves sent down the Reminder﴾ — i.e., We Ourselves sent down that Reminder, which they denied and because of which they attributed madness to you. ﴿And indeed We are its guardians﴾ — against everything unbefitting it, such as distortion, alteration, addition, omission, and the like.

In this there is a severe warning to those who deny it and mock the Messenger of God (ﷺ). It was said that the pronoun in "its" refers to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), but the first is more suitable to the context.

Then (glory be to Him) mentioned that the custom of such disbelievers with their prophets was the same, as consolation for the Messenger of God (ﷺ). So He said: ﴿We certainly sent (messengers) before you﴾ — i.e., messengers, the word being omitted because the sending indicates it: messengers who existed before you ﴿among the sects of the former peoples﴾ — among their nations, their followers, and all their factions and groups.

Al-Farra' said: *shiya'* (sects) means the community following one another in what they agree upon. Its root is from *sha'ahu*, meaning he followed him. Its being attributed to "the former peoples" is either an attribution of a qualifier to the qualified, according to some grammarians, or an ellipsis of the qualified, according to others.

﴿No messenger came to them but they mocked him.﴾ I.e., no messenger among the messengers came to his followers except that they mocked him, as these disbelievers do with Muhammad (ﷺ). The clause ﴿but they mocked him﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, or in the nominative position as a qualifier of "messenger," or in the genitive position as a qualifier of it according to its form, not its location.

﴿Thus We let it enter into the hearts of the criminals.﴾ I.e., in the same way as We made it enter the hearts of those who mocked their messengers, We let the Reminder — i.e., the Reminder — enter into the hearts of the criminals. So the demonstrative refers to what the preceding speech indicates, namely the sending of revelation accompanied by mockery. *Al-salk* means the insertion of one thing into another, like a thread into a needle, as al-Zajjaj said. He said: the meaning is, just as We did to the criminals who mocked, We make error enter the hearts of the criminals.

The clause ﴿They do not believe in it﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ﴿We let it enter﴾, i.e., they do not believe in the Reminder that We have sent down. It is also permissible that it be a new sentence explaining what precedes it, in which case it has no grammatical position. It was also said that the pronoun in ﴿We let it enter﴾ refers to mockery, and the pronoun in ﴿They do not believe in it﴾ refers to the Reminder, but this is far-fetched. The more correct view is that both pronouns refer to the Reminder.

﴿Though the way of the former peoples has already passed.﴾ I.e., their established way, which God ordained regarding their destruction, has already passed, since they did what they did of denial and mockery.

Al-Zajjaj said: the sunna of God regarding the former peoples has passed, namely that He let disbelief and error enter their hearts.

Then God (glory be to Him) related their persistence in disbelief and their determination in denial and mockery.

Then He said: ﴿Even if We opened for them a gate into the heaven﴾, meaning for these obstinate opponents of Muhammad (ﷺ), who denied him and mocked him, ﴿a gate from the sky﴾, meaning from its known gates, and We enabled them to ascend through it, ﴿and they continued to ascend through it﴾, meaning through that gate, ﴿ascending﴾, meaning climbing, whether by means of an instrument or without one, until they witnessed what is in the heaven of the wonders of the malakut (the unseen dominion of God), which no denier could deny and no obstinate person could oppose upon seeing it. It has also been said that the pronoun in ﴿they continued﴾ refers to the angels, meaning that the angels continued to ascend through that gate while the unbelievers watched them and observed their ascent through that gate. ﴿They would surely say﴾, meaning the unbelievers, because of the extremity of their obstinacy and the increase of their defiance: ﴿Our eyes have only been intoxicated.﴾ Ibn Kathir read ﴿سُكِرَتْ﴾ (sukirat) with light emphasis, while the rest read it with the doubled letter (sukkirat). It is from the intoxication of drink, or from sakr, which means blocking the senses, as one says sakara al-nahr (he dammed the river) when he dams it and holds it back from flowing. The second meaning was preferred on the basis of the light reading.

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: ﴿سُكِّرَتْ﴾ means "it was covered and veiled." From this is the verse of the poet:

*And a sun rose over them, with a helmet of mail,*
*and the eye of the heat-haze began to be blocked.*

This is also the view of Abu 'Ubayd and Abu 'Ubayda. It is also narrated from Abu 'Amr that it is from the intoxication of drink, meaning that what covers their sight overtook them as intoxication overtakes the drunkard, covering his intellect. It has also been said that the meaning of ﴿سُكِّرَتْ﴾ is "held back," as already mentioned. From this is the verse of Aws ibn Hajar:

*So I remained awake through a night of watching,*
*and it was neither clear nor blocked.*

Al-Nahhas said: these views are close in meaning.

﴿Rather, we are a people who have been bewitched﴾: they turned away from their statement "our eyes have been intoxicated," and then claimed that they were bewitched, meaning that Muhammad (ﷺ) had bewitched them.

In this there is an explanation of their great obstinacy, which nothing whatsoever can turn them away from. When they see a sign that obliges them to believe in God, His angels, His books and His messengers, they attribute to their eyes that their perception of it is not real, due to an intoxicating impediment, or they claim that their intellects have been bewitched, so their perception has become unsound. Whoever has reached this degree of stubbornness, admonition will not benefit him, and he will not be guided by any sign.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid concerning God's words ﴿These are the verses of the Book﴾ that he said: "the Torah and the Gospel."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated concerning ﴿These are the verses of the Book﴾ that he said: "the books that came before the Qur'an." Concerning ﴿and a clear Qur'an﴾ he said: "Clear, by God, its guidance, its rectitude and its good."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud and some of the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning God's words ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims﴾, that he said: "The polytheists wished on the Day of Badr, when their necks were struck and they were presented to the Fire, that they had been believers in Muhammad (ﷺ)."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Mas'ud concerning the verse that he said: "This is about the people of Hell when they see them coming out of the Fire."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Hannad ibn al-Sari in al-Zuhd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th wa al-Nushur narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "God continues to intercede, and to admit, and to intercede, and to show mercy, until He says: whoever was a Muslim, let him enter Paradise. That is His words: ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims﴾."

Ibn al-Mubarak in al-Zuhd, Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Anas that they discussed this verse, ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims﴾, and they said: "This is when God gathers the people of sins, from among the Muslims and the polytheists, into the Fire, and the polytheists say: what your worship benefited you is nothing. Then God becomes angry on their behalf and brings them out by His grace and mercy."

al-Tabarani in al-Awsat and Ibn Mardawayh narrated with a chain, which al-Suyuti said is sahih, from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Some people of my community will be punished for their sins and will remain in the Fire as long as God wills. Then the people of polytheism will reproach them, saying: We do not see that what you believed in benefited you. So no one who affirms God's oneness will remain but God will bring him out of the Fire." Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited: ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims﴾.

Ibn Abi 'Asim in al-Sunna, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar.

Ishaq ibn Rahawayh, Ibn Hibban, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar as well.

Hannad ibn al-Sari, al-Tabarani in al-Awsat and Abu Nu'aym narrated from Anas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar also.

There are hadiths on the matter that specify the cause of the revelation of this verse.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Zayd concerning God's words ﴿Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves﴾, the verse, that he said: "These are the disbelievers."

He also narrated from Abu Malik concerning God's words, ﴿Leave them﴾, that he said: "Let them alone."

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Zuhri concerning God's words ﴿No nation precedes its term, nor do they delay﴾, that he said: "We hold that when its term arrives, it is not delayed an hour nor advanced. As for what has not yet reached its term, God delays whom He wills and advances whom He wills."

I say: this statement of al-Zuhri has no substance and no benefit in it.

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Dahhak concerning God's words ﴿O you to whom the Reminder has been sent﴾, that he said: "The Qur'an."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid concerning God's words ﴿We do not send down the angels except with truth﴾, that he said: "With the message and the punishment."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi concerning God's words ﴿And they would not have been reprieved﴾, that he said: "And they would not, even if the angels descended, have been reprieved from being punished."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid concerning ﴿And indeed We are its guardians﴾, that he said: "With Us."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning God's words ﴿among the sects of the former peoples﴾, that he said: "the nations of the former peoples."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Anas concerning God's words ﴿Thus We insert it into the hearts of the criminals﴾, that he said: "Polytheism, We insert it into the hearts of the polytheists."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatada something similar.

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from al-Hasan something similar also.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatada concerning ﴿And the example of the former peoples has already passed﴾, that he said: "the events of God concerning those among the nations who passed away."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Jurayj concerning God's words ﴿and they continued to ascend through it﴾, that Ibn Jurayj said: Ibn 'Abbas said: "The angels continued to ascend, and they looked at them, and said: ﴿Our eyes have only been intoxicated﴾." He said: "It is the Quraysh who say it."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated concerning the verse, also from Ibn 'Abbas, that he said: "If We opened for them a gate from the gates of heaven, and the angels continued to ascend through it, going and coming in disagreement about it, the people of polytheism would say: our sight has only been taken away and confused for us, and we have only been bewitched."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid concerning ﴿Our eyes have been intoxicated﴾ that he said: "They have been blocked."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatada something similar, and said: "Whoever reads ﴿سُكِرَتْ﴾ with the light emphasis, he means ﴿سُحِرَتْ﴾ (suhirat), 'bewitched'."

Its classification as Meccan is agreed upon, as al-Qurtubi said.

Al-Nahhas in his *Nasikh* (on abrogation, *naskh*) and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Surat al-Hijr was revealed in Mecca."

Ibn Mardawayh also narrated from Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr something similar.

﴿Alif. Lam. Ra. These are the verses of the Book and a clear Qur'an.﴾ ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims.﴾ ﴿Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves, and let hope distract them. They will soon know.﴾ ﴿We never destroyed a town without its having a known decreed term.﴾ ﴿No nation can hasten its term, nor can it delay it.﴾ ﴿They say: "O you to whom the Reminder has been sent, you are surely a madman!"﴾ ﴿"Why do you not bring us angels, if you are among the truthful?"﴾ ﴿We do not send down the angels except with truth, and then they would not be given respite.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We Ourselves sent down the Reminder, and indeed We are its guardians.﴾ ﴿We certainly sent (messengers) before you among the sects of the former peoples.﴾ ﴿No messenger came to them but they mocked him.﴾ ﴿Thus We let it enter into the hearts of the criminals.﴾ ﴿They do not believe in it, though the way of the former peoples has already passed.﴾ ﴿Even if We opened for them a gate in the sky and they kept ascending through it,﴾ ﴿they would say, "Our eyes have only been dazzled; rather, we are a people bewitched."﴾

Regarding His words ﴿Alif Lam Ra﴾: the discussion of it has already been given in full in its proper place. The demonstrative in ﴿These are the verses﴾ refers to what the surah contains of verses. The definiteness in "the Book" is said to be generic (*li-l-jins*), meaning the category of previous scriptures. It was also said that it refers to the Qur'an; the mention of "the Qur'an" after "the Book" does not undermine this, since it has been said that He combined the two names for it. It was also said that "the Book" means this surah itself. The indefiniteness of "a Qur'an" is for magnification, i.e., the complete Qur'an.

﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims.﴾ Nafi' and Asim read the *ba'* of *rubama* with a light (single) pronunciation, while the rest read it with emphasis (doubled). Both are dialects. Abu Hatim said: "The people of the Hijaz pronounce it lightly," and from this is the poet's verse:

*Rubba darbatin bi-saifin saqilin / bayna Busra wa-ta'natin najla'*
(Many a blow with a polished sword between Busra and a wide-gaping spear-thrust.)

The Tamim and Rabi'a tribes pronounce it with emphasis. The *ta'* (feminine) may be added to it, and its original use is for the few, though it may also be used for the many. The Kufans said: the meaning is that the disbelievers will wish, at many times, that they had been Muslims. From this is the poet's verse:

*Rubba rafdin harraqtahu dhalika al-yawma / wa-asra min ma'shari aqyali*
(How many a gift you poured out that day, and captives from a folk of chieftains.)

It was also said that *rubba* here is for paucity, because they wished for this at some times and not at all times, being occupied with the punishment. It is said that *ma* here is attached to *rubba* to prepare it to enter upon a verb. It was also said that it is an indefinite noun meaning "a thing." *Rubba* enters here upon the future, although it only enters upon the past, because what is awaited in His report (glory be to Him) is like what has occurred and is certain; it is as if it were said: "Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims," i.e., submitting to His judgment, humbly accepting it, among its people.

This wishing from them occurs at the time of their death or on the Day of Resurrection. The meaning is that when the matter became clear to them, and the falsity of what they had been upon of disbelief became evident, and that religion before God (glory be to Him) is Islam, with no religion other than it, this wishing arose in them, which neither fattens nor satisfies hunger. Rather, it is merely regret, remorse, and self-reproach over what they neglected regarding God's right. It was said that this wishing from them occurs upon witnessing their state and the state of the Muslims. It was also said that it occurs when the sinners among the monotheists come out of the Fire. The apparent meaning is that this wishing is constantly present in them at every moment after the matter has been revealed to them.

﴿Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves﴾: this is a threat to them, i.e., leave them to what you are engaged in of commanding and forbidding them. They will never mend their ways, nor leave falsehood, nor enter into truth. Rather, let them be with what they are occupied with: eating and enjoying the flower of this world. They are like cattle, which concern themselves only with that and occupy themselves with nothing else. The meaning is: leave them to what they are upon of occupation with eating and the like, with the goods of this world, and with hope distracting them from following you. "They will soon know" the outcome of their affair and the evil of their deeds.

In this there is a threat and a rebuke of an immeasurable measure (p-٧٥٦). It is said: *alhahu kadha*, i.e., he occupied him; *lahā 'ani al-shay'i yalhu*, i.e., he was distracted from the thing. The meaning is: hope occupied them away from following the truth. They continued in empty hopes and false wishes until the morning became clear to the one who has two eyes, the matter was uncovered, and they saw the punishment on the Day of Resurrection. At that time they will taste the evil consequence of what they did.

The three verbs are jussive because they are the answer to the imperative. This verse is abrogated (*mansukha*) by the verse of the sword.

﴿We never destroyed a town without its having a known decreed term.﴾ I.e., We never destroyed any town among the towns with any kind of punishment, ﴿except that﴾ — for that town there is a *kitab*, i.e., a fixed term that it cannot precede or delay, known, not unknown or forgotten. Thus, it is inconceivable that it could deviate from it in any way. The clause "for it is a Book" is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring to "town." Although it is indefinite, it has taken the status of a qualified noun because of the generality it carries. The *waw* distinguishes whether this clause is a circumstantial clause or a qualifier, for it specifies it as circumstantial, as in your saying: "my state is a man with a sword on his shoulder." It was also said that the clause is a qualifier of "town," and the *waw* serves to emphasize the adhesion between the qualifier and the qualified.

﴿No nation can hasten its term.﴾ I.e., no nation among the nations can precede its term, which has been set for it and written in the Preserved Tablet (*al-Lawh al-Mahfuz*). The meaning is that its destruction does not come before its term arrives. ﴿Nor can they delay it.﴾ I.e., they cannot be late in relation to it, so that their destruction comes after the appointed term has passed. The use of the verb in the masculine plural form is for the sake of meaning, with predominance, and for the sake of the rhyme endings; therefore the prepositional phrase has been omitted. The clause explains what precedes it, as if it were said: this respite should not deceive the wise, for every nation has a specific time for the descent of punishment, which neither precedes nor follows.

The explanation of "term" (*ajal*) has already been given at the beginning of Surat al-An'am.

Then, when He had finished with the threat against the disbelievers, He began to explain some of their obstinacy in disbelief and their persistence in error, together with its inclusion of a demonstration of their disbelief in the one to whom the Book was revealed, after demonstrating their disbelief in the Book. So He said: ﴿They say: "O you to whom the Reminder has been sent!"﴾ I.e., the disbelievers of Mecca said, addressing the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and mocking him, since they affirmed for him the sending down of the Reminder while in reality they denied it most strongly and rejected it most emphatically. Or they meant by ﴿O you to whom the Reminder has been sent﴾ — according to his claim and in accordance with what he asserts — ﴿you are surely a madman!﴾ I.e., because of this claim you make, that you are a messenger of God commanded to convey His rulings, you are surely mad, for no one who was sane would claim such a great claim in their view. Their saying this to Muhammad (ﷺ) is like the saying of Pharaoh: ﴿Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is surely mad﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:27].

﴿Why do you not bring us angels﴾: *law ma* is a particle of urging, composed of *law*, which conveys wishing, and the extra *ma*. Thus the whole conveys urging to the action into which it enters. The meaning is: "Why do you not bring us angels, so that they may bear witness to your truthfulness, if you are among the truthful?"

Al-Farra' said: the *mim* in *lawma* is a substitute for the *lam* in *lawla*. Al-Kisa'i said: *lawla* and *lawma* are the same in statement and in question. Al-Nahhas said: *lawma*, *lawla*, and *halla* are one and the same. It was also said: the meaning is "Why do you not bring us angels, so that they would punish us for our denial of you?"

﴿We do not send down the angels except with truth﴾: it was read as "*ma nunazzilu*" with the *nun*, in the active voice, with God (glory be to Him) as the agent, so it is from "sending down" (*tanzil*). The meaning in this reading: God (glory be to Him) said, answering the disbelievers when they asked for the angels to come to them: "We do not send down the angels except with truth," i.e., sending them down clothed in the truth that justifies their sending down to them in what the divine wisdom and the lordly will require. What you have proposed is not something for which the sending down of angels is justified. It was also read *nunzilu* (without doubling), from *inzal* (causing to descend). It was read also *ma tanazzalu* with the *ta'* at the beginning, as an imperfect verb in the intensive form, active voice, from *tanzil*, with one of the two *ta'*s elided, i.e., *tatanazzalu* (they descend). It was also read with the *ta'* at the beginning as an imperfect verb in the passive voice. It was said that the meaning of "except with truth" is: except with the Qur'an; it was said: with the message; it was said: with punishment. (And they would not be given respite.) There is an ellipsis in the speech; the estimated meaning is: "Had We sent down the angels, they would have been hastened to punishment, and they would not have been given respite." Thus the clause mentioned is the answer to the omitted conditional clause.

Then He denounced the disbelievers' mockery of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) by their saying: ﴿O you to whom the Reminder has been sent, you are surely a madman!﴾ So He (glory be to Him) said: ﴿Indeed, We Ourselves sent down the Reminder﴾ — i.e., We Ourselves sent down that Reminder, which they denied and because of which they attributed madness to you. ﴿And indeed We are its guardians﴾ — against everything unbefitting it, such as distortion, alteration, addition, omission, and the like.

In this there is a severe warning to those who deny it and mock the Messenger of God (ﷺ). It was said that the pronoun in "its" refers to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), but the first is more suitable to the context.

Then (glory be to Him) mentioned that the custom of such disbelievers with their prophets was the same, as consolation for the Messenger of God (ﷺ). So He said: ﴿We certainly sent (messengers) before you﴾ — i.e., messengers, the word being omitted because the sending indicates it: messengers who existed before you ﴿among the sects of the former peoples﴾ — among their nations, their followers, and all their factions and groups.

Al-Farra' said: *shiya'* (sects) means the community following one another in what they agree upon. Its root is from *sha'ahu*, meaning he followed him. Its being attributed to "the former peoples" is either an attribution of a qualifier to the qualified, according to some grammarians, or an ellipsis of the qualified, according to others.

﴿No messenger came to them but they mocked him.﴾ I.e., no messenger among the messengers came to his followers except that they mocked him, as these disbelievers do with Muhammad (ﷺ). The clause ﴿but they mocked him﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, or in the nominative position as a qualifier of "messenger," or in the genitive position as a qualifier of it according to its form, not its location.

﴿Thus We let it enter into the hearts of the criminals.﴾ I.e., in the same way as We made it enter the hearts of those who mocked their messengers, We let the Reminder — i.e., the Reminder — enter into the hearts of the criminals. So the demonstrative refers to what the preceding speech indicates, namely the sending of revelation accompanied by mockery. *Al-salk* means the insertion of one thing into another, like a thread into a needle, as al-Zajjaj said. He said: the meaning is, just as We did to the criminals who mocked, We make error enter the hearts of the criminals.

The clause ﴿They do not believe in it﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ﴿We let it enter﴾, i.e., they do not believe in the Reminder that We have sent down. It is also permissible that it be a new sentence explaining what precedes it, in which case it has no grammatical position. It was also said that the pronoun in ﴿We let it enter﴾ refers to mockery, and the pronoun in ﴿They do not believe in it﴾ refers to the Reminder, but this is far-fetched. The more correct view is that both pronouns refer to the Reminder.

﴿Though the way of the former peoples has already passed.﴾ I.e., their established way, which God ordained regarding their destruction, has already passed, since they did what they did of denial and mockery.

Al-Zajjaj said: the sunna of God regarding the former peoples has passed, namely that He let disbelief and error enter their hearts.

Then God (glory be to Him) related their persistence in disbelief and their determination in denial and mockery.

Then He said: ﴿Even if We opened for them a gate into the heaven﴾, meaning for these obstinate opponents of Muhammad (ﷺ), who denied him and mocked him, ﴿a gate from the sky﴾, meaning from its known gates, and We enabled them to ascend through it, ﴿and they continued to ascend through it﴾, meaning through that gate, ﴿ascending﴾, meaning climbing, whether by means of an instrument or without one, until they witnessed what is in the heaven of the wonders of the malakut (the unseen dominion of God), which no denier could deny and no obstinate person could oppose upon seeing it. It has also been said that the pronoun in ﴿they continued﴾ refers to the angels, meaning that the angels continued to ascend through that gate while the unbelievers watched them and observed their ascent through that gate. ﴿They would surely say﴾, meaning the unbelievers, because of the extremity of their obstinacy and the increase of their defiance: ﴿Our eyes have only been intoxicated.﴾ Ibn Kathir read ﴿سُكِرَتْ﴾ (sukirat) with light emphasis, while the rest read it with the doubled letter (sukkirat). It is from the intoxication of drink, or from sakr, which means blocking the senses, as one says sakara al-nahr (he dammed the river) when he dams it and holds it back from flowing. The second meaning was preferred on the basis of the light reading.

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: ﴿سُكِّرَتْ﴾ means "it was covered and veiled." From this is the verse of the poet:

*And a sun rose over them, with a helmet of mail,*
*and the eye of the heat-haze began to be blocked.*

This is also the view of Abu 'Ubayd and Abu 'Ubayda. It is also narrated from Abu 'Amr that it is from the intoxication of drink, meaning that what covers their sight overtook them as intoxication overtakes the drunkard, covering his intellect. It has also been said that the meaning of ﴿سُكِّرَتْ﴾ is "held back," as already mentioned. From this is the verse of Aws ibn Hajar:

*So I remained awake through a night of watching,*
*and it was neither clear nor blocked.*

Al-Nahhas said: these views are close in meaning.

﴿Rather, we are a people who have been bewitched﴾: they turned away from their statement "our eyes have been intoxicated," and then claimed that they were bewitched, meaning that Muhammad (ﷺ) had bewitched them.

In this there is an explanation of their great obstinacy, which nothing whatsoever can turn them away from. When they see a sign that obliges them to believe in God, His angels, His books and His messengers, they attribute to their eyes that their perception of it is not real, due to an intoxicating impediment, or they claim that their intellects have been bewitched, so their perception has become unsound. Whoever has reached this degree of stubbornness, admonition will not benefit him, and he will not be guided by any sign.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid concerning God's words ﴿These are the verses of the Book﴾ that he said: "the Torah and the Gospel."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated concerning ﴿These are the verses of the Book﴾ that he said: "the books that came before the Qur'an." Concerning ﴿and a clear Qur'an﴾ he said: "Clear, by God, its guidance, its rectitude and its good."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud and some of the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning God's words ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims﴾, that he said: "The polytheists wished on the Day of Badr, when their necks were struck and they were presented to the Fire, that they had been believers in Muhammad (ﷺ)."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Mas'ud concerning the verse that he said: "This is about the people of Hell when they see them coming out of the Fire."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Hannad ibn al-Sari in al-Zuhd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th wa al-Nushur narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "God continues to intercede, and to admit, and to intercede, and to show mercy, until He says: whoever was a Muslim, let him enter Paradise. That is His words: ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims﴾."

Ibn al-Mubarak in al-Zuhd, Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Anas that they discussed this verse, ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims﴾, and they said: "This is when God gathers the people of sins, from among the Muslims and the polytheists, into the Fire, and the polytheists say: what your worship benefited you is nothing. Then God becomes angry on their behalf and brings them out by His grace and mercy."

al-Tabarani in al-Awsat and Ibn Mardawayh narrated with a chain, which al-Suyuti said is sahih, from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Some people of my community will be punished for their sins and will remain in the Fire as long as God wills. Then the people of polytheism will reproach them, saying: We do not see that what you believed in benefited you. So no one who affirms God's oneness will remain but God will bring him out of the Fire." Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited: ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims﴾.

Ibn Abi 'Asim in al-Sunna, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar.

Ishaq ibn Rahawayh, Ibn Hibban, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar as well.

Hannad ibn al-Sari, al-Tabarani in al-Awsat and Abu Nu'aym narrated from Anas, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar also.

There are hadiths on the matter that specify the cause of the revelation of this verse.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Zayd concerning God's words ﴿Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves﴾, the verse, that he said: "These are the disbelievers."

He also narrated from Abu Malik concerning God's words, ﴿Leave them﴾, that he said: "Let them alone."

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Zuhri concerning God's words ﴿No nation precedes its term, nor do they delay﴾, that he said: "We hold that when its term arrives, it is not delayed an hour nor advanced. As for what has not yet reached its term, God delays whom He wills and advances whom He wills."

I say: this statement of al-Zuhri has no substance and no benefit in it.

Ibn Jarir narrated from al-Dahhak concerning God's words ﴿O you to whom the Reminder has been sent﴾, that he said: "The Qur'an."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid concerning God's words ﴿We do not send down the angels except with truth﴾, that he said: "With the message and the punishment."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi concerning God's words ﴿And they would not have been reprieved﴾, that he said: "And they would not, even if the angels descended, have been reprieved from being punished."

Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid concerning ﴿And indeed We are its guardians﴾, that he said: "With Us."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning God's words ﴿among the sects of the former peoples﴾, that he said: "the nations of the former peoples."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Anas concerning God's words ﴿Thus We insert it into the hearts of the criminals﴾, that he said: "Polytheism, We insert it into the hearts of the polytheists."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatada something similar.

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from al-Hasan something similar also.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatada concerning ﴿And the example of the former peoples has already passed﴾, that he said: "the events of God concerning those among the nations who passed away."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Jurayj concerning God's words ﴿and they continued to ascend through it﴾, that Ibn Jurayj said: Ibn 'Abbas said: "The angels continued to ascend, and they looked at them, and said: ﴿Our eyes have only been intoxicated﴾." He said: "It is the Quraysh who say it."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated concerning the verse, also from Ibn 'Abbas, that he said: "If We opened for them a gate from the gates of heaven, and the angels continued to ascend through it, going and coming in disagreement about it, the people of polytheism would say: our sight has only been taken away and confused for us, and we have only been bewitched."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid concerning ﴿Our eyes have been intoxicated﴾ that he said: "They have been blocked."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Qatada something similar, and said: "Whoever reads ﴿سُكِرَتْ﴾ with the light emphasis, he means ﴿سُحِرَتْ﴾ (suhirat), 'bewitched'."

Its classification as Meccan is agreed upon, as al-Qurtubi said.

Al-Nahhas in his *Nasikh* (on abrogation, *naskh*) and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Surat al-Hijr was revealed in Mecca."

Ibn Mardawayh also narrated from Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr something similar.

﴿Alif. Lam. Ra. These are the verses of the Book and a clear Qur'an.﴾ ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims.﴾ ﴿Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves, and let hope distract them. They will soon know.﴾ ﴿We never destroyed a town without its having a known decreed term.﴾ ﴿No nation can hasten its term, nor can it delay it.﴾ ﴿They say: "O you to whom the Reminder has been sent, you are surely a madman!"﴾ ﴿"Why do you not bring us angels, if you are among the truthful?"﴾ ﴿We do not send down the angels except with truth, and then they would not be given respite.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We Ourselves sent down the Reminder, and indeed We are its guardians.﴾ ﴿We certainly sent (messengers) before you among the sects of the former peoples.﴾ ﴿No messenger came to them but they mocked him.﴾ ﴿Thus We let it enter into the hearts of the criminals.﴾ ﴿They do not believe in it, though the way of the former peoples has already passed.﴾ ﴿Even if We opened for them a gate in the sky and they kept ascending through it,﴾ ﴿they would say, "Our eyes have only been dazzled; rather, we are a people bewitched."﴾

Regarding His words ﴿Alif Lam Ra﴾: the discussion of it has already been given in full in its proper place. The demonstrative in ﴿These are the verses﴾ refers to what the surah contains of verses. The definiteness in "the Book" is said to be generic (*li-l-jins*), meaning the category of previous scriptures. It was also said that it refers to the Qur'an; the mention of "the Qur'an" after "the Book" does not undermine this, since it has been said that He combined the two names for it. It was also said that "the Book" means this surah itself. The indefiniteness of "a Qur'an" is for magnification, i.e., the complete Qur'an.

﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims.﴾ Nafi' and Asim read the *ba'* of *rubama* with a light (single) pronunciation, while the rest read it with emphasis (doubled). Both are dialects. Abu Hatim said: "The people of the Hijaz pronounce it lightly," and from this is the poet's verse:

*Rubba darbatin bi-saifin saqilin / bayna Busra wa-ta'natin najla'*
(Many a blow with a polished sword between Busra and a wide-gaping spear-thrust.)

The Tamim and Rabi'a tribes pronounce it with emphasis. The *ta'* (feminine) may be added to it, and its original use is for the few, though it may also be used for the many. The Kufans said: the meaning is that the disbelievers will wish, at many times, that they had been Muslims. From this is the poet's verse:

*Rubba rafdin harraqtahu dhalika al-yawma / wa-asra min ma'shari aqyali*
(How many a gift you poured out that day, and captives from a folk of chieftains.)

It was also said that *rubba* here is for paucity, because they wished for this at some times and not at all times, being occupied with the punishment. It is said that *ma* here is attached to *rubba* to prepare it to enter upon a verb. It was also said that it is an indefinite noun meaning "a thing." *Rubba* enters here upon the future, although it only enters upon the past, because what is awaited in His report (glory be to Him) is like what has occurred and is certain; it is as if it were said: "Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims," i.e., submitting to His judgment, humbly accepting it, among its people.

This wishing from them occurs at the time of their death or on the Day of Resurrection. The meaning is that when the matter became clear to them, and the falsity of what they had been upon of disbelief became evident, and that religion before God (glory be to Him) is Islam, with no religion other than it, this wishing arose in them, which neither fattens nor satisfies hunger. Rather, it is merely regret, remorse, and self-reproach over what they neglected regarding God's right. It was said that this wishing from them occurs upon witnessing their state and the state of the Muslims. It was also said that it occurs when the sinners among the monotheists come out of the Fire. The apparent meaning is that this wishing is constantly present in them at every moment after the matter has been revealed to them.

﴿Leave them to eat and enjoy themselves﴾: this is a threat to them, i.e., leave them to what you are engaged in of commanding and forbidding them. They will never mend their ways, nor leave falsehood, nor enter into truth. Rather, let them be with what they are occupied with: eating and enjoying the flower of this world. They are like cattle, which concern themselves only with that and occupy themselves with nothing else. The meaning is: leave them to what they are upon of occupation with eating and the like, with the goods of this world, and with hope distracting them from following you. "They will soon know" the outcome of their affair and the evil of their deeds.

In this there is a threat and a rebuke of an immeasurable measure (p-٧٥٦). It is said: *alhahu kadha*, i.e., he occupied him; *lahā 'ani al-shay'i yalhu*, i.e., he was distracted from the thing. The meaning is: hope occupied them away from following the truth. They continued in empty hopes and false wishes until the morning became clear to the one who has two eyes, the matter was uncovered, and they saw the punishment on the Day of Resurrection. At that time they will taste the evil consequence of what they did.

The three verbs are jussive because they are the answer to the imperative. This verse is abrogated (*mansukha*) by the verse of the sword.

﴿We never destroyed a town without its having a known decreed term.﴾ I.e., We never destroyed any town among the towns with any kind of punishment, ﴿except that﴾ — for that town there is a *kitab*, i.e., a fixed term that it cannot precede or delay, known, not unknown or forgotten. Thus, it is inconceivable that it could deviate from it in any way. The clause "for it is a Book" is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*hal*) referring to "town." Although it is indefinite, it has taken the status of a qualified noun because of the generality it carries. The *waw* distinguishes whether this clause is a circumstantial clause or a qualifier, for it specifies it as circumstantial, as in your saying: "my state is a man with a sword on his shoulder." It was also said that the clause is a qualifier of "town," and the *waw* serves to emphasize the adhesion between the qualifier and the qualified.

﴿No nation can hasten its term.﴾ I.e., no nation among the nations can precede its term, which has been set for it and written in the Preserved Tablet (*al-Lawh al-Mahfuz*). The meaning is that its destruction does not come before its term arrives. ﴿Nor can they delay it.﴾ I.e., they cannot be late in relation to it, so that their destruction comes after the appointed term has passed. The use of the verb in the masculine plural form is for the sake of meaning, with predominance, and for the sake of the rhyme endings; therefore the prepositional phrase has been omitted. The clause explains what precedes it, as if it were said: this respite should not deceive the wise, for every nation has a specific time for the descent of punishment, which neither precedes nor follows.

The explanation of "term" (*ajal*) has already been given at the beginning of Surat al-An'am.

Then, when He had finished with the threat against the disbelievers, He began to explain some of their obstinacy in disbelief and their persistence in error, together with its inclusion of a demonstration of their disbelief in the one to whom the Book was revealed, after demonstrating their disbelief in the Book. So He said: ﴿They say: "O you to whom the Reminder has been sent!"﴾ I.e., the disbelievers of Mecca said, addressing the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and mocking him, since they affirmed for him the sending down of the Reminder while in reality they denied it most strongly and rejected it most emphatically. Or they meant by ﴿O you to whom the Reminder has been sent﴾ — according to his claim and in accordance with what he asserts — ﴿you are surely a madman!﴾ I.e., because of this claim you make, that you are a messenger of God commanded to convey His rulings, you are surely mad, for no one who was sane would claim such a great claim in their view. Their saying this to Muhammad (ﷺ) is like the saying of Pharaoh: ﴿Indeed, your messenger who has been sent to you is surely mad﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:27].

﴿Why do you not bring us angels﴾: *law ma* is a particle of urging, composed of *law*, which conveys wishing, and the extra *ma*. Thus the whole conveys urging to the action into which it enters. The meaning is: "Why do you not bring us angels, so that they may bear witness to your truthfulness, if you are among the truthful?"

Al-Farra' said: the *mim* in *lawma* is a substitute for the *lam* in *lawla*. Al-Kisa'i said: *lawla* and *lawma* are the same in statement and in question. Al-Nahhas said: *lawma*, *lawla*, and *halla* are one and the same. It was also said: the meaning is "Why do you not bring us angels, so that they would punish us for our denial of you?"

﴿We do not send down the angels except with truth﴾: it was read as "*ma nunazzilu*" with the *nun*, in the active voice, with God (glory be to Him) as the agent, so it is from "sending down" (*tanzil*). The meaning in this reading: God (glory be to Him) said, answering the disbelievers when they asked for the angels to come to them: "We do not send down the angels except with truth," i.e., sending them down clothed in the truth that justifies their sending down to them in what the divine wisdom and the lordly will require. What you have proposed is not something for which the sending down of angels is justified. It was also read *nunzilu* (without doubling), from *inzal* (causing to descend). It was read also *ma tanazzalu* with the *ta'* at the beginning, as an imperfect verb in the intensive form, active voice, from *tanzil*, with one of the two *ta'*s elided, i.e., *tatanazzalu* (they descend). It was also read with the *ta'* at the beginning as an imperfect verb in the passive voice. It was said that the meaning of "except with truth" is: except with the Qur'an; it was said: with the message; it was said: with punishment. (And they would not be given respite.) There is an ellipsis in the speech; the estimated meaning is: "Had We sent down the angels, they would have been hastened to punishment, and they would not have been given respite." Thus the clause mentioned is the answer to the omitted conditional clause.

Then He denounced the disbelievers' mockery of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) by their saying: ﴿O you to whom the Reminder has been sent, you are surely a madman!﴾ So He (glory be to Him) said: ﴿Indeed, We Ourselves sent down the Reminder﴾ — i.e., We Ourselves sent down that Reminder, which they denied and because of which they attributed madness to you. ﴿And indeed We are its guardians﴾ — against everything unbefitting it, such as distortion, alteration, addition, omission, and the like.

In this there is a severe warning to those who deny it and mock the Messenger of God (ﷺ). It was said that the pronoun in "its" refers to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), but the first is more suitable to the context.

Then (glory be to Him) mentioned that the custom of such disbelievers with their prophets was the same, as consolation for the Messenger of God (ﷺ). So He said: ﴿We certainly sent (messengers) before you﴾ — i.e., messengers, the word being omitted because the sending indicates it: messengers who existed before you ﴿among the sects of the former peoples﴾ — among their nations, their followers, and all their factions and groups.

Al-Farra' said: *shiya'* (sects) means the community following one another in what they agree upon. Its root is from *sha'ahu*, meaning he followed him. Its being attributed to "the former peoples" is either an attribution of a qualifier to the qualified, according to some grammarians, or an ellipsis of the qualified, according to others.

﴿No messenger came to them but they mocked him.﴾ I.e., no messenger among the messengers came to his followers except that they mocked him, as these disbelievers do with Muhammad (ﷺ). The clause ﴿but they mocked him﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, or in the nominative position as a qualifier of "messenger," or in the genitive position as a qualifier of it according to its form, not its location.

﴿Thus We let it enter into the hearts of the criminals.﴾ I.e., in the same way as We made it enter the hearts of those who mocked their messengers, We let the Reminder — i.e., the Reminder — enter into the hearts of the criminals. So the demonstrative refers to what the preceding speech indicates, namely the sending of revelation accompanied by mockery. *Al-salk* means the insertion of one thing into another, like a thread into a needle, as al-Zajjaj said. He said: the meaning is, just as We did to the criminals who mocked, We make error enter the hearts of the criminals.

The clause ﴿They do not believe in it﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ﴿We let it enter﴾, i.e., they do not believe in the Reminder that We have sent down. It is also permissible that it be a new sentence explaining what precedes it, in which case it has no grammatical position. It was also said that the pronoun in ﴿We let it enter﴾ refers to mockery, and the pronoun in ﴿They do not believe in it﴾ refers to the Reminder, but this is far-fetched. The more correct view is that both pronouns refer to the Reminder.

﴿Though the way of the former peoples has already passed.﴾ I.e., their established way, which God ordained regarding their destruction, has already passed, since they did what they did of denial and mockery.

Al-Zajjaj said: the sunna of God regarding the former peoples has passed, namely that He let disbelief and error enter their hearts.

Then God (glory be to Him) related their persistence in disbelief and their determination in denial and mockery.

Then He said: ﴿Even if We opened for them a gate into the heaven﴾, meaning for these obstinate opponents of Muhammad (ﷺ), who denied him and mocked him, ﴿a gate from the sky﴾, meaning from its known gates, and We enabled them to ascend through it, ﴿and they continued to ascend through it﴾, meaning through that gate, ﴿ascending﴾, meaning climbing, whether by means of an instrument or without one, until they witnessed what is in the heaven of the wonders of the malakut (the unseen dominion of God), which no denier could deny and no obstinate person could oppose upon seeing it. It has also been said that the pronoun in ﴿they continued﴾ refers to the angels, meaning that the angels continued to ascend through that gate while the unbelievers watched them and observed their ascent through that gate. ﴿They would surely say﴾, meaning the unbelievers, because of the extremity of their obstinacy and the increase of their defiance: ﴿Our eyes have only been intoxicated.﴾ Ibn Kathir read ﴿سُكِرَتْ﴾ (sukirat) with light emphasis, while the rest read it with the doubled letter (sukkirat). It is from the intoxication of drink, or from sakr, which means blocking the senses, as one says sakara al-nahr (he dammed the river) when he dams it and holds it back from flowing. The second meaning was preferred on the basis of the light reading.

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: ﴿سُكِّرَتْ﴾ means "it was covered and veiled." From this is the verse of the poet:

*And a sun rose over them, with a helmet of mail,*
*and the eye of the heat-haze began to be blocked.*

This is also the view of Abu 'Ubayd and Abu 'Ubayda. It is also narrated from Abu 'Amr that it is from the intoxication of drink, meaning that what covers their sight overtook them as intoxication overtakes the drunkard, covering his intellect. It has also been said that the meaning of ﴿سُكِّرَتْ﴾ is "held back," as already mentioned. From this is the verse of Aws ibn Hajar:

*So I remained awake through a night of watching,*
*and it was neither clear nor blocked.*

Al-Nahhas said: these views are close in meaning.

﴿Rather, we are a people who have been bewitched﴾: they turned away from their statement "our eyes have been intoxicated," and then claimed that they were bewitched, meaning that Muhammad (ﷺ) had bewitched them.

In this there is an explanation of their great obstinacy, which nothing whatsoever can turn them away from. When they see a sign that obliges them to believe in God, His angels, His books and His messengers, they attribute to their eyes that their perception of it is not real, due to an intoxicating impediment, or they claim that their intellects have been bewitched, so their perception has become unsound. Whoever has reached this degree of stubbornness, admonition will not benefit him, and he will not be guided by any sign.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Mujahid concerning God's words ﴿These are the verses of the Book﴾ that he said: "the Torah and the Gospel."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated concerning ﴿These are the verses of the Book﴾ that he said: "the books that came before the Qur'an." Concerning ﴿and a clear Qur'an﴾ he said: "Clear, by God, its guidance, its rectitude and its good."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud and some of the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning God's words ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims﴾, that he said: "The polytheists wished on the Day of Badr, when their necks were struck and they were presented to the Fire, that they had been believers in Muhammad (ﷺ)."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Mas'ud concerning the verse that he said: "This is about the people of Hell when they see them coming out of the Fire."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Hannad ibn al-Sari in al-Zuhd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th wa al-Nushur narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "God continues to intercede, and to admit, and to intercede, and to show mercy, until He says: whoever was a Muslim, let him enter Paradise. That is His words: ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims﴾."

Ibn al-Mubarak in al-Zuhd, Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Bayhaqi in al-Ba'th narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Anas that they discussed this verse, ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims﴾, and they said: "This is when God gathers the people of sins, from among the Muslims and the polytheists, into the Fire, and the polytheists say: what your worship benefited you is nothing. Then God becomes angry on their behalf and brings them out by His grace and mercy."

al-Tabarani in al-Awsat and Ibn Mardawayh narrated with a chain, which al-Suyuti said is sahih, from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Some people of my community will be punished for their sins and will remain in the Fire as long as God wills. Then the people of polytheism will reproach them, saying: We do not see that what you believed in benefited you. So no one who affirms God's oneness will remain but God will bring him out of the Fire." Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited: ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims﴾.
