﴿قَالُوا لَا تَوْجَلْ﴾ (They said, "Do not be fearful"): that is, the angels said, "Do not fear." It is also read as "lā tājal," and "lā tawjal" is from awjalahu, meaning: he frightened him. The clause ﴿إِنَّا نُبَشِّرُكَ بِغُلَامٍ عَلِيمٍ﴾ (Indeed, we give you good news of a knowing boy) is a new sentence giving the reason for the prohibition against fear. "ʿAlīm" means one of abundant knowledge. It was also said: it means "ḥalīm" (forbearing), as occurs in another place in the Qur'an. This boy is Isaac, as has preceded in Hud. He did not name him here, nor did he mention the good news of Jacob, being content with what had passed.

﴿قَالَ أَبَشَّرْتُمُونِي﴾ (He said, "Do you give me good news...?"): the majority read it with the interrogative alif (ʾabashshartumūnī). Al-Aʿmash read "bashshartumūnī" without the alif.

﴿عَلَىٰ أَن مَّسَّنِيَ الْكِبَرُ﴾ (...when old age has touched me): the clause is in the position of a circumstantial state, meaning: along with the state of old age and senility.

﴿فَبِمَ تُبَشِّرُونَ﴾ (Then by what will you give me good news?) is an interrogative of wonder, as if he was amazed at the child being born to him despite his having reached the decrepitude after which it is customary that no child is born. The meaning is: "By what thing do you give me good news? For good news of what is not customary is not valid."

Nafi' read ﴿تُبَشِّرُونِ﴾ (tubashshirūnī) with a kasra on the nūn and lightening (the shadda omitted), leaving the kasra to indicate the elided yāʾ.

Ibn Kathir and Ibn Muhaysin read it with a kasra on the nūn and a shadda, by assimilating the nūn into the nūn, its original form being tubashshirūnanī.

The rest read ﴿تُبَشِّرُونَ﴾ (tubashshirūna) with a fatḥa on the nūn.

﴿قَالُوا بَشَّرْنَاكَ بِالْحَقِّ﴾ (They said, "We have given you good news in truth"): that is, with certainty that admits no doubt, for that is the promise of God, and He does not fail in His promise, and nothing is impossible for Him, for He is capable of everything. ﴿فَلَا تَكُن مِّنَ الْقَانِطِينَ﴾ (So do not be among the despairing). The majority read it this way with the alif (al-qānitīn).

Al-Aʿmash and Yahya ibn Wathhab read ﴿مِنَ الْقَنِطِينَ﴾ (al-qanitīn) without the alif, and this is related from Abu ʿAmr, meaning: among those who despair of what We have given you good news of.

﴿قَالَ وَمَن يَقْنَطُ مِن رَّحْمَةِ رَبِّهِ إِلَّا الضَّالُّونَ﴾ (He said, "And who despairs of the mercy of his Lord except those astray?"): "yaqnaṭu" was read with a fatḥa on the nūn, and with a kasra, and both are dialects. A ḍamma on the nūn is also related. "Al-ḍāllūn" means those who deny, or those who err and stray from the path of correctness. That is: "I only found the child unlikely because of my old age, not because I despair of the mercy of my Lord."

Then he asked them about the reason God had sent them: ﴿قَالَ فَمَا خَطْبُكُمْ أَيُّهَا الْمُرْسَلُونَ﴾ (He said, "Then what is your business, O messengers?"). "Khaṭb" means a grave matter and a great affair. That is: what is your matter and your business, and what is it that you have come with other than what you have given me good news of? It seems he understood that their coming was not merely for the good news, but that they had another matter for which they were sent.

﴿قَالُوا إِنَّا أُرْسِلْنَا إِلَىٰ قَوْمٍ مُّجْرِمِينَ﴾ (They said, "Indeed, we have been sent to a wicked people"): that is, to a people who commit crimes, which includes association with God and what is lesser than it. These people are the people of Lot.

Then He excepted from them those who were not criminals, saying: ﴿إِلَّا آلَ لُوطٍ﴾ (except the family of Lot). This is a connected exception (istithnāʾ muttaṣil), because it is from the pronoun in "mujrimīn." Had it been from "qawm," it would have been a disconnected exception (munqaṭiʿ), since they had been described as criminals, and the family of Lot were not criminals. Then He mentioned what the family of Lot would be specially honored with, because they had not joined the people in their crimes, saying: ﴿إِنَّا لَمُنَجُّوهُمْ أَجْمَعِينَ﴾ (Indeed, We will surely save them all), that is, the family of Lot, who are his followers and the people of his religion. This clause is a new sentence on the assumption that the exception is connected, as if it was said: "What will be the state of the family of Lot?" So He said, "Indeed, We will surely save them all." But on the assumption that the exception is disconnected, it is a predicate (khabar), meaning: "But the family of Lot are saved from Our punishment."

Ḥamza and al-Kisa'i read ﴿لَمُنجُوهُمْ﴾ (lamunjūhum) with lightening, from anjā. The rest read it with the shadda, from najjā.

This last reading was chosen by Abu ʿUbayda and Abu Ḥatim. Tanjiyah and injā' both mean deliverance from what others have fallen into.

﴿إِلَّا امْرَأَتَهُ﴾ (except his wife): this exception is from the pronoun in "munjūhum," excluding her from those who are delivered, meaning: except his wife, who is not among those We deliver but among those We destroy. It was also said: the exception is from "the family of Lot" with respect to what was ruled for them of deliverance. The meaning is: they said, "Indeed, we have been sent to a wicked people to destroy them, except the family of Lot. Indeed, We will save them, except his wife, for she is among those who will be destroyed."

The meaning of ﴿قَدَّرْنَا إِنَّهَا لَمِنَ الْغَابِرِينَ﴾ (We have decreed that she will be among those who remain behind) is: We decided and judged that she is among those who remain in the punishment along with the disbelievers. "Al-ghābir" means the remaining one. The poet said:

*Do not sweep the she-camels of their remaining milk, for you do not know who will bear the young.*

"Al-ighbār" means the remnants of milk.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of "qaddarnā" is "we arranged," and it is close in meaning to "qaḍaynā" (we decreed). The original sense of taqdīr is making a thing to the measure of sufficiency.

ʿĀṣim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr and al-Mufaḍḍal, read "qadarnā" with lightening, and the rest read it with the shadda.

Al-Harawi said: the two have the same meaning. The decreeing was attributed to the angels, although it is an act of God, glorified is He, because of their nearness to God.

﴿فَلَمَّا جَاءَ آلَ لُوطٍ الْمُرْسَلُونَ﴾ (So when the messengers came to the family of Lot): this clause is a new sentence explaining the destruction of those who deserve destruction and the deliverance of those who deserve salvation.

﴿قَالَ إِنَّكُمْ قَوْمٌ مُّنكَرُونَ﴾ (He said, "Indeed, you are a people unknown [to me]"): that is, Lot said, addressing them, "Indeed, you are a people unknown," meaning: I do not know you, rather I disown you.

﴿قَالُوا بَلْ جِئْنَاكَ بِمَا كَانُوا فِيهِ يَمْتَرُونَ﴾ (They said, "Rather, we have brought you that about which they had been disputing"): that is, the punishment about which they had been doubting. So the turning away (iḍrāb) is from his claim that they had come with something he disowned. It is as if they said: "We have not come to you with what occurred to your mind of the hateful, rather we have come to you with what brings you joy, which is their punishment, which you warned them of, while they denied you."

﴿وَأَتَيْنَاكَ بِالْحَقِّ﴾ (And We have brought you the truth): that is, with certainty that admits no doubt or hesitation, which is the punishment descending upon them without fail. ﴿وَإِنَّا لَصَادِقُونَ﴾ (And indeed, We are truthful) in that report which We have informed you of.

The explanation of His saying ﴿فَأَسْرِ بِأَهْلِكَ بِقِطْعٍ مِّنَ اللَّيْلِ﴾ (So travel with your family during a part of the night) has already passed in surah Hud. ﴿وَاتَّبِعْ أَدْبَارَهُمْ﴾ (And follow behind them): that is, be behind them, driving them on, so that none of them lags behind and is struck by the punishment. ﴿وَلَا يَلْتَفِتْ مِنكُمْ أَحَدٌ﴾ (And let not one of you look back): that is, neither you nor any of them should turn around and see what punishment has befallen them, lest he become occupied with looking at it, and slow down from the swiftness of the journey and from distancing himself from the abodes of the wrongdoers. It was also said: the meaning of "lā yaltafit" is "lā yatakhalladh" (let no one fall behind). ﴿وَامْضُوا حَيْثُ تُؤْمَرُونَ﴾ (And proceed to where you are commanded): that is, to the direction in which God, glorified is He, commanded you to proceed, which is the direction of the Levant (al-Sham). It was also said: Egypt; it was also said: a village of the villages of Lot; and it was also said: the land of the Friend (al-Khalil, Abraham).

﴿وَقَضَيْنَا إِلَيْهِ﴾ (And We conveyed to him): that is, We revealed to Lot ﴿ذَلِكَ الْأَمْرَ﴾ (that matter), which is the destruction of his people. Then He explained it with His saying: ﴿أَنَّ دَابِرَ هَٰؤُلَاءِ مَقْطُوعٌ مُّصْبِحِينَ﴾ (that the last of these people would be cut off at daybreak). Al-Zajjaj said: the position of "anna" is accusative, and it is a substitute (badal) for ﴿ذَلِكَ الْأَمْرَ﴾. "Al-dābir" is the last one, meaning: the last of them who remains will be destroyed at the time of morning. The accusative of "muṣbiḥīn" is a circumstantial state, meaning: while they are entering upon the time of morning. A similar expression is His saying: ﴿فَقُطِعَ دَابِرُ الْقَوْمِ الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا﴾ [al-An'am: 45] (So the last of the people who did wrong was cut off).

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Dahhak, regarding His saying "āminīn" (secure), that he said: they were secure from death, so they do not die, nor do they grow old, nor do they fall ill, nor do they become naked, nor do they become hungry.

Ibn Jarir related from ʿAlī regarding ﴿وَنَزَعْنَا مَا فِي صُدُورِهِم مِّنْ غِلٍّ﴾ that he said: "It is enmity."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Mardawayh related from al-Hasan al-Basri that he said: ʿAlī ibn Abi Talib said: "By God, it was about us that the people of Paradise were revealed: ﴿وَنَزَعْنَا مَا فِي صُدُورِهِم مِّنْ غِلٍّ إِخْوَانًا عَلَىٰ سُرُرٍ مُّتَقَابِلِينَ﴾ (And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts, as brothers, on couches facing one another)."

Ibn 'Asakir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him concerning this verse, saying: It was revealed concerning three Arab tribes: Banu Hashim, Banu Taym, and Banu 'Adi, concerning me and Abu Bakr and 'Umar.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from Kathir al-Nawwa', who said: I said to Abu Ja'far, "So-and-so narrated to me from 'Ali ibn al-Husayn that this verse was revealed concerning Abu Bakr, 'Umar, and 'Ali: ﴿And We removed whatever resentment was in their breasts﴾." He said: "By Allah, it was indeed revealed concerning them. And concerning whom else would it be revealed, if not them?" I said: "And what is this resentment?" He said: "It is the resentment of the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period of ignorance). Banu Taym, Banu 'Adi, and Banu Hashim had enmity between them in the Jahiliyyah. When these people embraced Islam, they loved one another. Then Abu Bakr was seized by a pain in his side, so 'Ali began to warm his hand and rub it on Abu Bakr's side, and this verse was revealed."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'Ali, through several chains, that he said to Ibn Talhah: "I hope that I and your father will be among those concerning whom Allah said: ﴿And We removed whatever resentment was in their breasts﴾, the verse." A man from Hamdan said: "Allah is more just than that." 'Ali cried out at him with a cry by which the palace shook, and said: "Then who, if we are not those?"

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'Ali that he said: "I hope that I, 'Uthman, al-Zubayr, and Talhah will be among those concerning whom Allah said: ﴿And We removed whatever resentment was in their breasts﴾."

Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn 'Asakir narrated through the route of al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning this verse, that he said: It was revealed concerning ten: Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Uthman, 'Ali, Talhah, al-Zubayr, Sa'd, Sa'id, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, and 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it from Abu Salih as a mawquf (a statement ending with a Companion, not traced to the Prophet).

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Hannad, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, concerning His saying: ﴿upon couches facing one another﴾, that he said: "None of them sees the nape of another."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated it from Mujahid, from Ibn 'Abbas.

Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Abu al-Qasim al-Baghawi, Ibn Mardawayh, and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from Zayd ibn Abi Awfa, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came out to us and recited this verse: ﴿as brothers upon couches facing one another﴾, and said: 'Those who love one another for the sake of Allah in Paradise, looking at one another.'"

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi, concerning His saying: ﴿No fatigue will touch them therein﴾, that he said: "The hardship and harm."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated through the route of 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, from a man among the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) looked down upon us from the gate through which the Banu Shaybah enter, and said: 'Do I not see you laughing?' Then he turned away, and when he reached al-Hajar, he came back backwards (al-qahqara) and said: 'When I went out, Jibril came and said: O Muhammad, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: Why do you cause My servants to despair? ﴿Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful, and that My punishment is the painful punishment﴾.'"

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mus'ab ibn Thabit, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) passed by some of his Companions who were laughing, and said: 'Remember Paradise and remember the Fire.' Then ﴿Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ was revealed."

Al-Tabarani, al-Bazzar, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) passed by... " and he mentioned something similar.

al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others narrated from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah created mercy on the day He created it as one hundred mercies. He retained with Himself ninety-nine mercies and sent down to His creation, all of them, one mercy. If the disbeliever knew all of the mercy that is with Allah, he would not despair of His mercy; and if the believer knew all of the punishment that is with Allah, he would not feel safe from the Fire."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from 'Ikrimah concerning ﴿They said: Do not fear﴾, that it means: do not be afraid.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi concerning ﴿of those who despair﴾, that he said: "Those who have given up hope."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah concerning ﴿Indeed, she is among those who remain behind﴾, meaning: those who remain in the punishment of Allah.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid concerning His saying: ﴿Indeed, you are a people unknown﴾, that he said: "Lot did not recognize them." And concerning His saying: ﴿about which they used to doubt﴾, he said: "With the punishment of the people of Lot."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatadah concerning ﴿about which they used to doubt﴾, that he said: "They were in doubt."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatadah concerning His saying: ﴿And follow their backs﴾, that he said: "He was commanded to be behind his family, following their backs at the end of them when they walked."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi concerning ﴿And proceed where you are commanded﴾ (p-766), that he said: "Allah brought them out to Syria."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Zayd concerning ﴿And We decreed that matter to him﴾, that he said: "We revealed it to him."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿that the last of these people will be cut off﴾, meaning the complete destruction of them.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 15, verses 45–66 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, ﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be in gardens and springs﴾: that is, those who guard against associating partners with God, as said by the majority of the Companions and the Successors (al-Tabi'un). It was also said: they are those who guard against all acts of disobedience. "Gardens" means orchards, and "springs" means rivers.

"ʿUyūn" (springs) was read with a ḍamma on the ʿayn, according to the original form, and with a kasra out of consideration for the yāʾ. The construction may allow that (a) the gardens and springs belong to all the God-fearing collectively, or (b) each one of them has gardens and springs, or (c) each one of them has a garden and a spring.

As for ﴿ادْخُلُوها﴾ (udkhulūhā, "enter it"), the majority read it in the imperative form, with the implied phrase "it was said", meaning: it will be said to them, "Enter it."

Al-Hasan, Abu al-ʿĀliya, and what is related from Yaʿqūb read it with a ḍamma on the hamza, as a separate verb (ʾudkhilūhā, "they were made to enter"), and with a fatḥa on the kha', as a passive verb, meaning: God caused them to enter it.

It has been said: since they are already in gardens and springs, how can it be said to them, "Enter it," according to the reading of the majority? The command to enter suggests that they were not in it.

The answer given is that the meaning is: when they have arrived at the gardens, and then move from one of them to another, it will be said to them, upon their arrival at the one they wish to move to, "Enter it." The meaning of ﴿بِسَلامٍ آمِنِينَ﴾ (with peace, secure) is: with safety from calamities and security from fears. Or it means: greeting one another with peace, or being greeted with peace by the angels, or by God, Mighty and Majestic.

﴿وَنَزَعْنا مَا فِي صُدُورِهِم مِّنْ غِلٍّ﴾ (And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts): al-ghill means spite and enmity, and its explanation has already passed in surah al-Aʿraf. The accusative of ﴿إِخْوَانًا﴾ (as brothers) is in the position of a circumstantial state (ḥāl), meaning: brothers in religion and in mutual affection. ﴿عَلَى سُرُرٍ مُّتَقَابِلِينَ﴾ (on couches, facing one another) means: while they are on couches, and in a specific form, which is facing one another, each one looking at the face of the other. Al-sururr is the plural of sarīr (couch). It was also said: it is an elevated seat prepared for joy. From this comes the saying "sirr al-wadi," for the best place in it.

﴿لَا يَمَسُّهُمْ فِيهَا نَصَبٌ﴾ (No fatigue will touch them therein): that is, weariness and exhaustion, because the causes of that do not exist in Paradise, since it is pure bliss and unmixed pleasure, which they obtain with ease. Their desires come to them without earning or effort. Rather, merely by the thought of wanting a thing passing through their hearts, that thing comes to them readily and freely. ﴿وَمَا هُم مِّنْهَا بِمُخْرَجِينَ﴾ (nor will they ever be removed from it): forever. In this everlasting eternity, and in their knowledge of it, lies the completeness of pleasure and the perfection of bliss, for the knowledge of one who is in blessing and pleasure that it will end after a time would necessarily disturb his bliss and cloud his pleasure.

Then, after relating to us what the God-fearing have with Him of great reward and abundant recompense, He, glorified is He, said: ﴿نَبِّئْ عِبَادِي أَنِّي أَنَا الْغَفُورُ الرَّحِيمُ﴾ (Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful). That is: tell them, O Muhammad, that I am the One who forgives their sins abundantly, and is abundantly merciful to them, just as I have decreed upon Myself that My mercy precedes My wrath. O God, make us among Your servants whom You have favored with forgiveness and admitted under the vast expanse of Your mercy.

Then, when He, glorified is He, commanded His Messenger to inform His servants of this great glad tidings (p-764), He commanded him to mention to them something that includes warning and caution, so that hope and fear would be combined, and good news and warning would be balanced, so that they would be both hopeful and fearful. So He said: ﴿وَأَنَّ عَذَابِي هُوَ الْعَذَابُ الْأَلِيمُ﴾ (And that My punishment is the painful punishment), that is, the one that causes great pain. When God combined these two matters for His servants, the good news and the warning, they came to a middle state between despair and hope. The best of affairs is their middle, and it is standing on the two feet of hope and fear, and between the two states of intimacy and awe.

The clause ﴿وَنَبِّئْهُمْ عَن ضَيْفِ إِبْرَاهِيمَ﴾ (And inform them about the guests of Abraham) is conjoined to the clause ﴿نَبِّئْ عِبَادِي﴾ (Inform My servants). That is: inform them of what happened to Abraham, the matter in which both hope and fear were combined for him, and the good news that was mixed with a kind of trepidation, so that they may take a lesson from it and know that this is God's way with His servants.

Also, since the story includes the deliverance of the believers and the destruction of the wrongdoers, this serves to confirm that He is the Forgiving, the Merciful, and that His punishment is the painful punishment. The explanation of this story has already passed in surah Hud.

The accusative of ﴿إِذْ دَخَلُوا عَلَيْهِ﴾ (when they entered upon him) is governed by an implied verb conjoined to ﴿نَبِّئْ عِبَادِي﴾, meaning: and mention to them their entering upon him. Or it is in the position of a circumstantial state (ḥāl). "Ḍayf" (guest) originally is a verbal noun (maṣdar), and that is why it is in the singular even though they were a group. It is called "ḍayf" because of its being attached to the host (muḍīf).

﴿فَقَالُوا سَلَامًا﴾ (They said, "Peace!"): that is, "We greet you with peace." ﴿قَالَ إِنَّا مِنكُمْ وَجِلُونَ﴾ (He said, "Indeed, we are fearful of you"): that is, fearful and frightened. He said this after he had brought the calf near to them and saw that they did not eat from it, as had preceded in surah Hud. ﴿فَلَمَّا رَأَىٰ أَيْدِيَهُمْ لَا تَصِلُ إِلَيْهِ نَكِرَهُمْ وَأَوْجَسَ مِنْهُمْ خِيفَةً﴾ [Hud: 70] (But when he saw that their hands did not reach it, he was suspicious of them and felt fear within himself). It was said: he disapproved of their greeting because it was not customary in their land. It was also said: he disapproved of their entering upon him without seeking permission.

﴿قَالُوا لَا تَوْجَلْ﴾ (They said, "Do not be fearful"): that is, the angels said, "Do not fear." It is also read as "lā tājal," and "lā tawjal" is from awjalahu, meaning: he frightened him. The clause ﴿إِنَّا نُبَشِّرُكَ بِغُلَامٍ عَلِيمٍ﴾ (Indeed, we give you good news of a knowing boy) is a new sentence giving the reason for the prohibition against fear. "ʿAlīm" means one of abundant knowledge. It was also said: it means "ḥalīm" (forbearing), as occurs in another place in the Qur'an. This boy is Isaac, as has preceded in Hud. He did not name him here, nor did he mention the good news of Jacob, being content with what had passed.

﴿قَالَ أَبَشَّرْتُمُونِي﴾ (He said, "Do you give me good news...?"): the majority read it with the interrogative alif (ʾabashshartumūnī). Al-Aʿmash read "bashshartumūnī" without the alif.

﴿عَلَىٰ أَن مَّسَّنِيَ الْكِبَرُ﴾ (...when old age has touched me): the clause is in the position of a circumstantial state, meaning: along with the state of old age and senility.

﴿فَبِمَ تُبَشِّرُونَ﴾ (Then by what will you give me good news?) is an interrogative of wonder, as if he was amazed at the child being born to him despite his having reached the decrepitude after which it is customary that no child is born. The meaning is: "By what thing do you give me good news? For good news of what is not customary is not valid."

Nafi' read ﴿تُبَشِّرُونِ﴾ (tubashshirūnī) with a kasra on the nūn and lightening (the shadda omitted), leaving the kasra to indicate the elided yāʾ.

Ibn Kathir and Ibn Muhaysin read it with a kasra on the nūn and a shadda, by assimilating the nūn into the nūn, its original form being tubashshirūnanī.

The rest read ﴿تُبَشِّرُونَ﴾ (tubashshirūna) with a fatḥa on the nūn.

﴿قَالُوا بَشَّرْنَاكَ بِالْحَقِّ﴾ (They said, "We have given you good news in truth"): that is, with certainty that admits no doubt, for that is the promise of God, and He does not fail in His promise, and nothing is impossible for Him, for He is capable of everything. ﴿فَلَا تَكُن مِّنَ الْقَانِطِينَ﴾ (So do not be among the despairing). The majority read it this way with the alif (al-qānitīn).

Al-Aʿmash and Yahya ibn Wathhab read ﴿مِنَ الْقَنِطِينَ﴾ (al-qanitīn) without the alif, and this is related from Abu ʿAmr, meaning: among those who despair of what We have given you good news of.

﴿قَالَ وَمَن يَقْنَطُ مِن رَّحْمَةِ رَبِّهِ إِلَّا الضَّالُّونَ﴾ (He said, "And who despairs of the mercy of his Lord except those astray?"): "yaqnaṭu" was read with a fatḥa on the nūn, and with a kasra, and both are dialects. A ḍamma on the nūn is also related. "Al-ḍāllūn" means those who deny, or those who err and stray from the path of correctness. That is: "I only found the child unlikely because of my old age, not because I despair of the mercy of my Lord."

Then he asked them about the reason God had sent them: ﴿قَالَ فَمَا خَطْبُكُمْ أَيُّهَا الْمُرْسَلُونَ﴾ (He said, "Then what is your business, O messengers?"). "Khaṭb" means a grave matter and a great affair. That is: what is your matter and your business, and what is it that you have come with other than what you have given me good news of? It seems he understood that their coming was not merely for the good news, but that they had another matter for which they were sent.

﴿قَالُوا إِنَّا أُرْسِلْنَا إِلَىٰ قَوْمٍ مُّجْرِمِينَ﴾ (They said, "Indeed, we have been sent to a wicked people"): that is, to a people who commit crimes, which includes association with God and what is lesser than it. These people are the people of Lot.

Then He excepted from them those who were not criminals, saying: ﴿إِلَّا آلَ لُوطٍ﴾ (except the family of Lot). This is a connected exception (istithnāʾ muttaṣil), because it is from the pronoun in "mujrimīn." Had it been from "qawm," it would have been a disconnected exception (munqaṭiʿ), since they had been described as criminals, and the family of Lot were not criminals. Then He mentioned what the family of Lot would be specially honored with, because they had not joined the people in their crimes, saying: ﴿إِنَّا لَمُنَجُّوهُمْ أَجْمَعِينَ﴾ (Indeed, We will surely save them all), that is, the family of Lot, who are his followers and the people of his religion. This clause is a new sentence on the assumption that the exception is connected, as if it was said: "What will be the state of the family of Lot?" So He said, "Indeed, We will surely save them all." But on the assumption that the exception is disconnected, it is a predicate (khabar), meaning: "But the family of Lot are saved from Our punishment."

Ḥamza and al-Kisa'i read ﴿لَمُنجُوهُمْ﴾ (lamunjūhum) with lightening, from anjā. The rest read it with the shadda, from najjā.

This last reading was chosen by Abu ʿUbayda and Abu Ḥatim. Tanjiyah and injā' both mean deliverance from what others have fallen into.

﴿إِلَّا امْرَأَتَهُ﴾ (except his wife): this exception is from the pronoun in "munjūhum," excluding her from those who are delivered, meaning: except his wife, who is not among those We deliver but among those We destroy. It was also said: the exception is from "the family of Lot" with respect to what was ruled for them of deliverance. The meaning is: they said, "Indeed, we have been sent to a wicked people to destroy them, except the family of Lot. Indeed, We will save them, except his wife, for she is among those who will be destroyed."

The meaning of ﴿قَدَّرْنَا إِنَّهَا لَمِنَ الْغَابِرِينَ﴾ (We have decreed that she will be among those who remain behind) is: We decided and judged that she is among those who remain in the punishment along with the disbelievers. "Al-ghābir" means the remaining one. The poet said:

*Do not sweep the she-camels of their remaining milk, for you do not know who will bear the young.*

"Al-ighbār" means the remnants of milk.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of "qaddarnā" is "we arranged," and it is close in meaning to "qaḍaynā" (we decreed). The original sense of taqdīr is making a thing to the measure of sufficiency.

ʿĀṣim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr and al-Mufaḍḍal, read "qadarnā" with lightening, and the rest read it with the shadda.

Al-Harawi said: the two have the same meaning. The decreeing was attributed to the angels, although it is an act of God, glorified is He, because of their nearness to God.

﴿فَلَمَّا جَاءَ آلَ لُوطٍ الْمُرْسَلُونَ﴾ (So when the messengers came to the family of Lot): this clause is a new sentence explaining the destruction of those who deserve destruction and the deliverance of those who deserve salvation.

﴿قَالَ إِنَّكُمْ قَوْمٌ مُّنكَرُونَ﴾ (He said, "Indeed, you are a people unknown [to me]"): that is, Lot said, addressing them, "Indeed, you are a people unknown," meaning: I do not know you, rather I disown you.

﴿قَالُوا بَلْ جِئْنَاكَ بِمَا كَانُوا فِيهِ يَمْتَرُونَ﴾ (They said, "Rather, we have brought you that about which they had been disputing"): that is, the punishment about which they had been doubting. So the turning away (iḍrāb) is from his claim that they had come with something he disowned. It is as if they said: "We have not come to you with what occurred to your mind of the hateful, rather we have come to you with what brings you joy, which is their punishment, which you warned them of, while they denied you."

﴿وَأَتَيْنَاكَ بِالْحَقِّ﴾ (And We have brought you the truth): that is, with certainty that admits no doubt or hesitation, which is the punishment descending upon them without fail. ﴿وَإِنَّا لَصَادِقُونَ﴾ (And indeed, We are truthful) in that report which We have informed you of.

The explanation of His saying ﴿فَأَسْرِ بِأَهْلِكَ بِقِطْعٍ مِّنَ اللَّيْلِ﴾ (So travel with your family during a part of the night) has already passed in surah Hud. ﴿وَاتَّبِعْ أَدْبَارَهُمْ﴾ (And follow behind them): that is, be behind them, driving them on, so that none of them lags behind and is struck by the punishment. ﴿وَلَا يَلْتَفِتْ مِنكُمْ أَحَدٌ﴾ (And let not one of you look back): that is, neither you nor any of them should turn around and see what punishment has befallen them, lest he become occupied with looking at it, and slow down from the swiftness of the journey and from distancing himself from the abodes of the wrongdoers. It was also said: the meaning of "lā yaltafit" is "lā yatakhalladh" (let no one fall behind). ﴿وَامْضُوا حَيْثُ تُؤْمَرُونَ﴾ (And proceed to where you are commanded): that is, to the direction in which God, glorified is He, commanded you to proceed, which is the direction of the Levant (al-Sham). It was also said: Egypt; it was also said: a village of the villages of Lot; and it was also said: the land of the Friend (al-Khalil, Abraham).

﴿وَقَضَيْنَا إِلَيْهِ﴾ (And We conveyed to him): that is, We revealed to Lot ﴿ذَلِكَ الْأَمْرَ﴾ (that matter), which is the destruction of his people. Then He explained it with His saying: ﴿أَنَّ دَابِرَ هَٰؤُلَاءِ مَقْطُوعٌ مُّصْبِحِينَ﴾ (that the last of these people would be cut off at daybreak). Al-Zajjaj said: the position of "anna" is accusative, and it is a substitute (badal) for ﴿ذَلِكَ الْأَمْرَ﴾. "Al-dābir" is the last one, meaning: the last of them who remains will be destroyed at the time of morning. The accusative of "muṣbiḥīn" is a circumstantial state, meaning: while they are entering upon the time of morning. A similar expression is His saying: ﴿فَقُطِعَ دَابِرُ الْقَوْمِ الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا﴾ [al-An'am: 45] (So the last of the people who did wrong was cut off).

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Dahhak, regarding His saying "āminīn" (secure), that he said: they were secure from death, so they do not die, nor do they grow old, nor do they fall ill, nor do they become naked, nor do they become hungry.

Ibn Jarir related from ʿAlī regarding ﴿وَنَزَعْنَا مَا فِي صُدُورِهِم مِّنْ غِلٍّ﴾ that he said: "It is enmity."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Mardawayh related from al-Hasan al-Basri that he said: ʿAlī ibn Abi Talib said: "By God, it was about us that the people of Paradise were revealed: ﴿وَنَزَعْنَا مَا فِي صُدُورِهِم مِّنْ غِلٍّ إِخْوَانًا عَلَىٰ سُرُرٍ مُّتَقَابِلِينَ﴾ (And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts, as brothers, on couches facing one another)."

Ibn 'Asakir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him concerning this verse, saying: It was revealed concerning three Arab tribes: Banu Hashim, Banu Taym, and Banu 'Adi, concerning me and Abu Bakr and 'Umar.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from Kathir al-Nawwa', who said: I said to Abu Ja'far, "So-and-so narrated to me from 'Ali ibn al-Husayn that this verse was revealed concerning Abu Bakr, 'Umar, and 'Ali: ﴿And We removed whatever resentment was in their breasts﴾." He said: "By Allah, it was indeed revealed concerning them. And concerning whom else would it be revealed, if not them?" I said: "And what is this resentment?" He said: "It is the resentment of the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period of ignorance). Banu Taym, Banu 'Adi, and Banu Hashim had enmity between them in the Jahiliyyah. When these people embraced Islam, they loved one another. Then Abu Bakr was seized by a pain in his side, so 'Ali began to warm his hand and rub it on Abu Bakr's side, and this verse was revealed."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'Ali, through several chains, that he said to Ibn Talhah: "I hope that I and your father will be among those concerning whom Allah said: ﴿And We removed whatever resentment was in their breasts﴾, the verse." A man from Hamdan said: "Allah is more just than that." 'Ali cried out at him with a cry by which the palace shook, and said: "Then who, if we are not those?"

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'Ali that he said: "I hope that I, 'Uthman, al-Zubayr, and Talhah will be among those concerning whom Allah said: ﴿And We removed whatever resentment was in their breasts﴾."

Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn 'Asakir narrated through the route of al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning this verse, that he said: It was revealed concerning ten: Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Uthman, 'Ali, Talhah, al-Zubayr, Sa'd, Sa'id, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, and 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it from Abu Salih as a mawquf (a statement ending with a Companion, not traced to the Prophet).

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Hannad, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, concerning His saying: ﴿upon couches facing one another﴾, that he said: "None of them sees the nape of another."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated it from Mujahid, from Ibn 'Abbas.

Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Abu al-Qasim al-Baghawi, Ibn Mardawayh, and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from Zayd ibn Abi Awfa, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came out to us and recited this verse: ﴿as brothers upon couches facing one another﴾, and said: 'Those who love one another for the sake of Allah in Paradise, looking at one another.'"

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi, concerning His saying: ﴿No fatigue will touch them therein﴾, that he said: "The hardship and harm."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated through the route of 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, from a man among the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) looked down upon us from the gate through which the Banu Shaybah enter, and said: 'Do I not see you laughing?' Then he turned away, and when he reached al-Hajar, he came back backwards (al-qahqara) and said: 'When I went out, Jibril came and said: O Muhammad, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: Why do you cause My servants to despair? ﴿Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful, and that My punishment is the painful punishment﴾.'"

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mus'ab ibn Thabit, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) passed by some of his Companions who were laughing, and said: 'Remember Paradise and remember the Fire.' Then ﴿Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ was revealed."

Al-Tabarani, al-Bazzar, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) passed by... " and he mentioned something similar.

al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others narrated from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah created mercy on the day He created it as one hundred mercies. He retained with Himself ninety-nine mercies and sent down to His creation, all of them, one mercy. If the disbeliever knew all of the mercy that is with Allah, he would not despair of His mercy; and if the believer knew all of the punishment that is with Allah, he would not feel safe from the Fire."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from 'Ikrimah concerning ﴿They said: Do not fear﴾, that it means: do not be afraid.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi concerning ﴿of those who despair﴾, that he said: "Those who have given up hope."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah concerning ﴿Indeed, she is among those who remain behind﴾, meaning: those who remain in the punishment of Allah.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid concerning His saying: ﴿Indeed, you are a people unknown﴾, that he said: "Lot did not recognize them." And concerning His saying: ﴿about which they used to doubt﴾, he said: "With the punishment of the people of Lot."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatadah concerning ﴿about which they used to doubt﴾, that he said: "They were in doubt."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatadah concerning His saying: ﴿And follow their backs﴾, that he said: "He was commanded to be behind his family, following their backs at the end of them when they walked."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi concerning ﴿And proceed where you are commanded﴾ (p-766), that he said: "Allah brought them out to Syria."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Zayd concerning ﴿And We decreed that matter to him﴾, that he said: "We revealed it to him."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿that the last of these people will be cut off﴾, meaning the complete destruction of them.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 15, verses 45–66 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, ﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be in gardens and springs﴾: that is, those who guard against associating partners with God, as said by the majority of the Companions and the Successors (al-Tabi'un). It was also said: they are those who guard against all acts of disobedience. "Gardens" means orchards, and "springs" means rivers.

"ʿUyūn" (springs) was read with a ḍamma on the ʿayn, according to the original form, and with a kasra out of consideration for the yāʾ. The construction may allow that (a) the gardens and springs belong to all the God-fearing collectively, or (b) each one of them has gardens and springs, or (c) each one of them has a garden and a spring.

As for ﴿ادْخُلُوها﴾ (udkhulūhā, "enter it"), the majority read it in the imperative form, with the implied phrase "it was said", meaning: it will be said to them, "Enter it."

Al-Hasan, Abu al-ʿĀliya, and what is related from Yaʿqūb read it with a ḍamma on the hamza, as a separate verb (ʾudkhilūhā, "they were made to enter"), and with a fatḥa on the kha', as a passive verb, meaning: God caused them to enter it.

It has been said: since they are already in gardens and springs, how can it be said to them, "Enter it," according to the reading of the majority? The command to enter suggests that they were not in it.

The answer given is that the meaning is: when they have arrived at the gardens, and then move from one of them to another, it will be said to them, upon their arrival at the one they wish to move to, "Enter it." The meaning of ﴿بِسَلامٍ آمِنِينَ﴾ (with peace, secure) is: with safety from calamities and security from fears. Or it means: greeting one another with peace, or being greeted with peace by the angels, or by God, Mighty and Majestic.

﴿وَنَزَعْنا مَا فِي صُدُورِهِم مِّنْ غِلٍّ﴾ (And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts): al-ghill means spite and enmity, and its explanation has already passed in surah al-Aʿraf. The accusative of ﴿إِخْوَانًا﴾ (as brothers) is in the position of a circumstantial state (ḥāl), meaning: brothers in religion and in mutual affection. ﴿عَلَى سُرُرٍ مُّتَقَابِلِينَ﴾ (on couches, facing one another) means: while they are on couches, and in a specific form, which is facing one another, each one looking at the face of the other. Al-sururr is the plural of sarīr (couch). It was also said: it is an elevated seat prepared for joy. From this comes the saying "sirr al-wadi," for the best place in it.

﴿لَا يَمَسُّهُمْ فِيهَا نَصَبٌ﴾ (No fatigue will touch them therein): that is, weariness and exhaustion, because the causes of that do not exist in Paradise, since it is pure bliss and unmixed pleasure, which they obtain with ease. Their desires come to them without earning or effort. Rather, merely by the thought of wanting a thing passing through their hearts, that thing comes to them readily and freely. ﴿وَمَا هُم مِّنْهَا بِمُخْرَجِينَ﴾ (nor will they ever be removed from it): forever. In this everlasting eternity, and in their knowledge of it, lies the completeness of pleasure and the perfection of bliss, for the knowledge of one who is in blessing and pleasure that it will end after a time would necessarily disturb his bliss and cloud his pleasure.

Then, after relating to us what the God-fearing have with Him of great reward and abundant recompense, He, glorified is He, said: ﴿نَبِّئْ عِبَادِي أَنِّي أَنَا الْغَفُورُ الرَّحِيمُ﴾ (Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful). That is: tell them, O Muhammad, that I am the One who forgives their sins abundantly, and is abundantly merciful to them, just as I have decreed upon Myself that My mercy precedes My wrath. O God, make us among Your servants whom You have favored with forgiveness and admitted under the vast expanse of Your mercy.

Then, when He, glorified is He, commanded His Messenger to inform His servants of this great glad tidings (p-764), He commanded him to mention to them something that includes warning and caution, so that hope and fear would be combined, and good news and warning would be balanced, so that they would be both hopeful and fearful. So He said: ﴿وَأَنَّ عَذَابِي هُوَ الْعَذَابُ الْأَلِيمُ﴾ (And that My punishment is the painful punishment), that is, the one that causes great pain. When God combined these two matters for His servants, the good news and the warning, they came to a middle state between despair and hope. The best of affairs is their middle, and it is standing on the two feet of hope and fear, and between the two states of intimacy and awe.

The clause ﴿وَنَبِّئْهُمْ عَن ضَيْفِ إِبْرَاهِيمَ﴾ (And inform them about the guests of Abraham) is conjoined to the clause ﴿نَبِّئْ عِبَادِي﴾ (Inform My servants). That is: inform them of what happened to Abraham, the matter in which both hope and fear were combined for him, and the good news that was mixed with a kind of trepidation, so that they may take a lesson from it and know that this is God's way with His servants.

Also, since the story includes the deliverance of the believers and the destruction of the wrongdoers, this serves to confirm that He is the Forgiving, the Merciful, and that His punishment is the painful punishment. The explanation of this story has already passed in surah Hud.

The accusative of ﴿إِذْ دَخَلُوا عَلَيْهِ﴾ (when they entered upon him) is governed by an implied verb conjoined to ﴿نَبِّئْ عِبَادِي﴾, meaning: and mention to them their entering upon him. Or it is in the position of a circumstantial state (ḥāl). "Ḍayf" (guest) originally is a verbal noun (maṣdar), and that is why it is in the singular even though they were a group. It is called "ḍayf" because of its being attached to the host (muḍīf).

﴿فَقَالُوا سَلَامًا﴾ (They said, "Peace!"): that is, "We greet you with peace." ﴿قَالَ إِنَّا مِنكُمْ وَجِلُونَ﴾ (He said, "Indeed, we are fearful of you"): that is, fearful and frightened. He said this after he had brought the calf near to them and saw that they did not eat from it, as had preceded in surah Hud. ﴿فَلَمَّا رَأَىٰ أَيْدِيَهُمْ لَا تَصِلُ إِلَيْهِ نَكِرَهُمْ وَأَوْجَسَ مِنْهُمْ خِيفَةً﴾ [Hud: 70] (But when he saw that their hands did not reach it, he was suspicious of them and felt fear within himself). It was said: he disapproved of their greeting because it was not customary in their land. It was also said: he disapproved of their entering upon him without seeking permission.

﴿قَالُوا لَا تَوْجَلْ﴾ (They said, "Do not be fearful"): that is, the angels said, "Do not fear." It is also read as "lā tājal," and "lā tawjal" is from awjalahu, meaning: he frightened him. The clause ﴿إِنَّا نُبَشِّرُكَ بِغُلَامٍ عَلِيمٍ﴾ (Indeed, we give you good news of a knowing boy) is a new sentence giving the reason for the prohibition against fear. "ʿAlīm" means one of abundant knowledge. It was also said: it means "ḥalīm" (forbearing), as occurs in another place in the Qur'an. This boy is Isaac, as has preceded in Hud. He did not name him here, nor did he mention the good news of Jacob, being content with what had passed.

﴿قَالَ أَبَشَّرْتُمُونِي﴾ (He said, "Do you give me good news...?"): the majority read it with the interrogative alif (ʾabashshartumūnī). Al-Aʿmash read "bashshartumūnī" without the alif.

﴿عَلَىٰ أَن مَّسَّنِيَ الْكِبَرُ﴾ (...when old age has touched me): the clause is in the position of a circumstantial state, meaning: along with the state of old age and senility.

﴿فَبِمَ تُبَشِّرُونَ﴾ (Then by what will you give me good news?) is an interrogative of wonder, as if he was amazed at the child being born to him despite his having reached the decrepitude after which it is customary that no child is born. The meaning is: "By what thing do you give me good news? For good news of what is not customary is not valid."

Nafi' read ﴿تُبَشِّرُونِ﴾ (tubashshirūnī) with a kasra on the nūn and lightening (the shadda omitted), leaving the kasra to indicate the elided yāʾ.

Ibn Kathir and Ibn Muhaysin read it with a kasra on the nūn and a shadda, by assimilating the nūn into the nūn, its original form being tubashshirūnanī.

The rest read ﴿تُبَشِّرُونَ﴾ (tubashshirūna) with a fatḥa on the nūn.

﴿قَالُوا بَشَّرْنَاكَ بِالْحَقِّ﴾ (They said, "We have given you good news in truth"): that is, with certainty that admits no doubt, for that is the promise of God, and He does not fail in His promise, and nothing is impossible for Him, for He is capable of everything. ﴿فَلَا تَكُن مِّنَ الْقَانِطِينَ﴾ (So do not be among the despairing). The majority read it this way with the alif (al-qānitīn).

Al-Aʿmash and Yahya ibn Wathhab read ﴿مِنَ الْقَنِطِينَ﴾ (al-qanitīn) without the alif, and this is related from Abu ʿAmr, meaning: among those who despair of what We have given you good news of.

﴿قَالَ وَمَن يَقْنَطُ مِن رَّحْمَةِ رَبِّهِ إِلَّا الضَّالُّونَ﴾ (He said, "And who despairs of the mercy of his Lord except those astray?"): "yaqnaṭu" was read with a fatḥa on the nūn, and with a kasra, and both are dialects. A ḍamma on the nūn is also related. "Al-ḍāllūn" means those who deny, or those who err and stray from the path of correctness. That is: "I only found the child unlikely because of my old age, not because I despair of the mercy of my Lord."

Then he asked them about the reason God had sent them: ﴿قَالَ فَمَا خَطْبُكُمْ أَيُّهَا الْمُرْسَلُونَ﴾ (He said, "Then what is your business, O messengers?"). "Khaṭb" means a grave matter and a great affair. That is: what is your matter and your business, and what is it that you have come with other than what you have given me good news of? It seems he understood that their coming was not merely for the good news, but that they had another matter for which they were sent.

﴿قَالُوا إِنَّا أُرْسِلْنَا إِلَىٰ قَوْمٍ مُّجْرِمِينَ﴾ (They said, "Indeed, we have been sent to a wicked people"): that is, to a people who commit crimes, which includes association with God and what is lesser than it. These people are the people of Lot.

Then He excepted from them those who were not criminals, saying: ﴿إِلَّا آلَ لُوطٍ﴾ (except the family of Lot). This is a connected exception (istithnāʾ muttaṣil), because it is from the pronoun in "mujrimīn." Had it been from "qawm," it would have been a disconnected exception (munqaṭiʿ), since they had been described as criminals, and the family of Lot were not criminals. Then He mentioned what the family of Lot would be specially honored with, because they had not joined the people in their crimes, saying: ﴿إِنَّا لَمُنَجُّوهُمْ أَجْمَعِينَ﴾ (Indeed, We will surely save them all), that is, the family of Lot, who are his followers and the people of his religion. This clause is a new sentence on the assumption that the exception is connected, as if it was said: "What will be the state of the family of Lot?" So He said, "Indeed, We will surely save them all." But on the assumption that the exception is disconnected, it is a predicate (khabar), meaning: "But the family of Lot are saved from Our punishment."

Ḥamza and al-Kisa'i read ﴿لَمُنجُوهُمْ﴾ (lamunjūhum) with lightening, from anjā. The rest read it with the shadda, from najjā.

This last reading was chosen by Abu ʿUbayda and Abu Ḥatim. Tanjiyah and injā' both mean deliverance from what others have fallen into.

﴿إِلَّا امْرَأَتَهُ﴾ (except his wife): this exception is from the pronoun in "munjūhum," excluding her from those who are delivered, meaning: except his wife, who is not among those We deliver but among those We destroy. It was also said: the exception is from "the family of Lot" with respect to what was ruled for them of deliverance. The meaning is: they said, "Indeed, we have been sent to a wicked people to destroy them, except the family of Lot. Indeed, We will save them, except his wife, for she is among those who will be destroyed."

The meaning of ﴿قَدَّرْنَا إِنَّهَا لَمِنَ الْغَابِرِينَ﴾ (We have decreed that she will be among those who remain behind) is: We decided and judged that she is among those who remain in the punishment along with the disbelievers. "Al-ghābir" means the remaining one. The poet said:

*Do not sweep the she-camels of their remaining milk, for you do not know who will bear the young.*

"Al-ighbār" means the remnants of milk.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of "qaddarnā" is "we arranged," and it is close in meaning to "qaḍaynā" (we decreed). The original sense of taqdīr is making a thing to the measure of sufficiency.

ʿĀṣim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr and al-Mufaḍḍal, read "qadarnā" with lightening, and the rest read it with the shadda.

Al-Harawi said: the two have the same meaning. The decreeing was attributed to the angels, although it is an act of God, glorified is He, because of their nearness to God.

﴿فَلَمَّا جَاءَ آلَ لُوطٍ الْمُرْسَلُونَ﴾ (So when the messengers came to the family of Lot): this clause is a new sentence explaining the destruction of those who deserve destruction and the deliverance of those who deserve salvation.

﴿قَالَ إِنَّكُمْ قَوْمٌ مُّنكَرُونَ﴾ (He said, "Indeed, you are a people unknown [to me]"): that is, Lot said, addressing them, "Indeed, you are a people unknown," meaning: I do not know you, rather I disown you.

﴿قَالُوا بَلْ جِئْنَاكَ بِمَا كَانُوا فِيهِ يَمْتَرُونَ﴾ (They said, "Rather, we have brought you that about which they had been disputing"): that is, the punishment about which they had been doubting. So the turning away (iḍrāb) is from his claim that they had come with something he disowned. It is as if they said: "We have not come to you with what occurred to your mind of the hateful, rather we have come to you with what brings you joy, which is their punishment, which you warned them of, while they denied you."

﴿وَأَتَيْنَاكَ بِالْحَقِّ﴾ (And We have brought you the truth): that is, with certainty that admits no doubt or hesitation, which is the punishment descending upon them without fail. ﴿وَإِنَّا لَصَادِقُونَ﴾ (And indeed, We are truthful) in that report which We have informed you of.

The explanation of His saying ﴿فَأَسْرِ بِأَهْلِكَ بِقِطْعٍ مِّنَ اللَّيْلِ﴾ (So travel with your family during a part of the night) has already passed in surah Hud. ﴿وَاتَّبِعْ أَدْبَارَهُمْ﴾ (And follow behind them): that is, be behind them, driving them on, so that none of them lags behind and is struck by the punishment. ﴿وَلَا يَلْتَفِتْ مِنكُمْ أَحَدٌ﴾ (And let not one of you look back): that is, neither you nor any of them should turn around and see what punishment has befallen them, lest he become occupied with looking at it, and slow down from the swiftness of the journey and from distancing himself from the abodes of the wrongdoers. It was also said: the meaning of "lā yaltafit" is "lā yatakhalladh" (let no one fall behind). ﴿وَامْضُوا حَيْثُ تُؤْمَرُونَ﴾ (And proceed to where you are commanded): that is, to the direction in which God, glorified is He, commanded you to proceed, which is the direction of the Levant (al-Sham). It was also said: Egypt; it was also said: a village of the villages of Lot; and it was also said: the land of the Friend (al-Khalil, Abraham).

﴿وَقَضَيْنَا إِلَيْهِ﴾ (And We conveyed to him): that is, We revealed to Lot ﴿ذَلِكَ الْأَمْرَ﴾ (that matter), which is the destruction of his people. Then He explained it with His saying: ﴿أَنَّ دَابِرَ هَٰؤُلَاءِ مَقْطُوعٌ مُّصْبِحِينَ﴾ (that the last of these people would be cut off at daybreak). Al-Zajjaj said: the position of "anna" is accusative, and it is a substitute (badal) for ﴿ذَلِكَ الْأَمْرَ﴾. "Al-dābir" is the last one, meaning: the last of them who remains will be destroyed at the time of morning. The accusative of "muṣbiḥīn" is a circumstantial state, meaning: while they are entering upon the time of morning. A similar expression is His saying: ﴿فَقُطِعَ دَابِرُ الْقَوْمِ الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا﴾ [al-An'am: 45] (So the last of the people who did wrong was cut off).

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Dahhak, regarding His saying "āminīn" (secure), that he said: they were secure from death, so they do not die, nor do they grow old, nor do they fall ill, nor do they become naked, nor do they become hungry.

Ibn Jarir related from ʿAlī regarding ﴿وَنَزَعْنَا مَا فِي صُدُورِهِم مِّنْ غِلٍّ﴾ that he said: "It is enmity."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Mardawayh related from al-Hasan al-Basri that he said: ʿAlī ibn Abi Talib said: "By God, it was about us that the people of Paradise were revealed: ﴿وَنَزَعْنَا مَا فِي صُدُورِهِم مِّنْ غِلٍّ إِخْوَانًا عَلَىٰ سُرُرٍ مُّتَقَابِلِينَ﴾ (And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts, as brothers, on couches facing one another)."

Ibn 'Asakir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him concerning this verse, saying: It was revealed concerning three Arab tribes: Banu Hashim, Banu Taym, and Banu 'Adi, concerning me and Abu Bakr and 'Umar.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from Kathir al-Nawwa', who said: I said to Abu Ja'far, "So-and-so narrated to me from 'Ali ibn al-Husayn that this verse was revealed concerning Abu Bakr, 'Umar, and 'Ali: ﴿And We removed whatever resentment was in their breasts﴾." He said: "By Allah, it was indeed revealed concerning them. And concerning whom else would it be revealed, if not them?" I said: "And what is this resentment?" He said: "It is the resentment of the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period of ignorance). Banu Taym, Banu 'Adi, and Banu Hashim had enmity between them in the Jahiliyyah. When these people embraced Islam, they loved one another. Then Abu Bakr was seized by a pain in his side, so 'Ali began to warm his hand and rub it on Abu Bakr's side, and this verse was revealed."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'Ali, through several chains, that he said to Ibn Talhah: "I hope that I and your father will be among those concerning whom Allah said: ﴿And We removed whatever resentment was in their breasts﴾, the verse." A man from Hamdan said: "Allah is more just than that." 'Ali cried out at him with a cry by which the palace shook, and said: "Then who, if we are not those?"

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'Ali that he said: "I hope that I, 'Uthman, al-Zubayr, and Talhah will be among those concerning whom Allah said: ﴿And We removed whatever resentment was in their breasts﴾."

Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn 'Asakir narrated through the route of al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning this verse, that he said: It was revealed concerning ten: Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Uthman, 'Ali, Talhah, al-Zubayr, Sa'd, Sa'id, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, and 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it from Abu Salih as a mawquf (a statement ending with a Companion, not traced to the Prophet).

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Hannad, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid, concerning His saying: ﴿upon couches facing one another﴾, that he said: "None of them sees the nape of another."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated it from Mujahid, from Ibn 'Abbas.

Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Abu al-Qasim al-Baghawi, Ibn Mardawayh, and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from Zayd ibn Abi Awfa, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came out to us and recited this verse: ﴿as brothers upon couches facing one another﴾, and said: 'Those who love one another for the sake of Allah in Paradise, looking at one another.'"

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi, concerning His saying: ﴿No fatigue will touch them therein﴾, that he said: "The hardship and harm."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated through the route of 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, from a man among the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) looked down upon us from the gate through which the Banu Shaybah enter, and said: 'Do I not see you laughing?' Then he turned away, and when he reached al-Hajar, he came back backwards (al-qahqara) and said: 'When I went out, Jibril came and said: O Muhammad, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: Why do you cause My servants to despair? ﴿Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful, and that My punishment is the painful punishment﴾.'"

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mus'ab ibn Thabit, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) passed by some of his Companions who were laughing, and said: 'Remember Paradise and remember the Fire.' Then ﴿Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ was revealed."

Al-Tabarani, al-Bazzar, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) passed by... " and he mentioned something similar.

al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others narrated from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah created mercy on the day He created it as one hundred mercies. He retained with Himself ninety-nine mercies and sent down to His creation, all of them, one mercy. If the disbeliever knew all of the mercy that is with Allah, he would not despair of His mercy; and if the believer knew all of the punishment that is with Allah, he would not feel safe from the Fire."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from 'Ikrimah concerning ﴿They said: Do not fear﴾, that it means: do not be afraid.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi concerning ﴿of those who despair﴾, that he said: "Those who have given up hope."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah concerning ﴿Indeed, she is among those who remain behind﴾, meaning: those who remain in the punishment of Allah.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Mujahid concerning His saying: ﴿Indeed, you are a people unknown﴾, that he said: "Lot did not recognize them." And concerning His saying: ﴿about which they used to doubt﴾, he said: "With the punishment of the people of Lot."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatadah concerning ﴿about which they used to doubt﴾, that he said: "They were in doubt."

'Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatadah concerning His saying: ﴿And follow their backs﴾, that he said: "He was commanded to be behind his family, following their backs at the end of them when they walked."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Suddi concerning ﴿And proceed where you are commanded﴾ (p-766), that he said: "Allah brought them out to Syria."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Zayd concerning ﴿And We decreed that matter to him﴾, that he said: "We revealed it to him."

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿that the last of these people will be cut off﴾, meaning the complete destruction of them.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 15, verses 45–66 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, ﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be in gardens and springs﴾: that is, those who guard against associating partners with God, as said by the majority of the Companions and the Successors (al-Tabi'un). It was also said: they are those who guard against all acts of disobedience. "Gardens" means orchards, and "springs" means rivers.

"ʿUyūn" (springs) was read with a ḍamma on the ʿayn, according to the original form, and with a kasra out of consideration for the yāʾ. The construction may allow that (a) the gardens and springs belong to all the God-fearing collectively, or (b) each one of them has gardens and springs, or (c) each one of them has a garden and a spring.

As for ﴿ادْخُلُوها﴾ (udkhulūhā, "enter it"), the majority read it in the imperative form, with the implied phrase "it was said", meaning: it will be said to them, "Enter it."

Al-Hasan, Abu al-ʿĀliya, and what is related from Yaʿqūb read it with a ḍamma on the hamza, as a separate verb (ʾudkhilūhā, "they were made to enter"), and with a fatḥa on the kha', as a passive verb, meaning: God caused them to enter it.

It has been said: since they are already in gardens and springs, how can it be said to them, "Enter it," according to the reading of the majority? The command to enter suggests that they were not in it.

The answer given is that the meaning is: when they have arrived at the gardens, and then move from one of them to another, it will be said to them, upon their arrival at the one they wish to move to, "Enter it." The meaning of ﴿بِسَلامٍ آمِنِينَ﴾ (with peace, secure) is: with safety from calamities and security from fears. Or it means: greeting one another with peace, or being greeted with peace by the angels, or by God, Mighty and Majestic.

﴿وَنَزَعْنا مَا فِي صُدُورِهِم مِّنْ غِلٍّ﴾ (And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts): al-ghill means spite and enmity, and its explanation has already passed in surah al-Aʿraf. The accusative of ﴿إِخْوَانًا﴾ (as brothers) is in the position of a circumstantial state (ḥāl), meaning: brothers in religion and in mutual affection. ﴿عَلَى سُرُرٍ مُّتَقَابِلِينَ﴾ (on couches, facing one another) means: while they are on couches, and in a specific form, which is facing one another, each one looking at the face of the other. Al-sururr is the plural of sarīr (couch). It was also said: it is an elevated seat prepared for joy. From this comes the saying "sirr al-wadi," for the best place in it.

﴿لَا يَمَسُّهُمْ فِيهَا نَصَبٌ﴾ (No fatigue will touch them therein): that is, weariness and exhaustion, because the causes of that do not exist in Paradise, since it is pure bliss and unmixed pleasure, which they obtain with ease. Their desires come to them without earning or effort. Rather, merely by the thought of wanting a thing passing through their hearts, that thing comes to them readily and freely. ﴿وَمَا هُم مِّنْهَا بِمُخْرَجِينَ﴾ (nor will they ever be removed from it): forever. In this everlasting eternity, and in their knowledge of it, lies the completeness of pleasure and the perfection of bliss, for the knowledge of one who is in blessing and pleasure that it will end after a time would necessarily disturb his bliss and cloud his pleasure.

Then, after relating to us what the God-fearing have with Him of great reward and abundant recompense, He, glorified is He, said: ﴿نَبِّئْ عِبَادِي أَنِّي أَنَا الْغَفُورُ الرَّحِيمُ﴾ (Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful). That is: tell them, O Muhammad, that I am the One who forgives their sins abundantly, and is abundantly merciful to them, just as I have decreed upon Myself that My mercy precedes My wrath. O God, make us among Your servants whom You have favored with forgiveness and admitted under the vast expanse of Your mercy.

Then, when He, glorified is He, commanded His Messenger to inform His servants of this great glad tidings (p-764), He commanded him to mention to them something that includes warning and caution, so that hope and fear would be combined, and good news and warning would be balanced, so that they would be both hopeful and fearful. So He said: ﴿وَأَنَّ عَذَابِي هُوَ الْعَذَابُ الْأَلِيمُ﴾ (And that My punishment is the painful punishment), that is, the one that causes great pain. When God combined these two matters for His servants, the good news and the warning, they came to a middle state between despair and hope. The best of affairs is their middle, and it is standing on the two feet of hope and fear, and between the two states of intimacy and awe.

The clause ﴿وَنَبِّئْهُمْ عَن ضَيْفِ إِبْرَاهِيمَ﴾ (And inform them about the guests of Abraham) is conjoined to the clause ﴿نَبِّئْ عِبَادِي﴾ (Inform My servants). That is: inform them of what happened to Abraham, the matter in which both hope and fear were combined for him, and the good news that was mixed with a kind of trepidation, so that they may take a lesson from it and know that this is God's way with His servants.

Also, since the story includes the deliverance of the believers and the destruction of the wrongdoers, this serves to confirm that He is the Forgiving, the Merciful, and that His punishment is the painful punishment. The explanation of this story has already passed in surah Hud.

The accusative of ﴿إِذْ دَخَلُوا عَلَيْهِ﴾ (when they entered upon him) is governed by an implied verb conjoined to ﴿نَبِّئْ عِبَادِي﴾, meaning: and mention to them their entering upon him. Or it is in the position of a circumstantial state (ḥāl). "Ḍayf" (guest) originally is a verbal noun (maṣdar), and that is why it is in the singular even though they were a group. It is called "ḍayf" because of its being attached to the host (muḍīf).

﴿فَقَالُوا سَلَامًا﴾ (They said, "Peace!"): that is, "We greet you with peace." ﴿قَالَ إِنَّا مِنكُمْ وَجِلُونَ﴾ (He said, "Indeed, we are fearful of you"): that is, fearful and frightened. He said this after he had brought the calf near to them and saw that they did not eat from it, as had preceded in surah Hud. ﴿فَلَمَّا رَأَىٰ أَيْدِيَهُمْ لَا تَصِلُ إِلَيْهِ نَكِرَهُمْ وَأَوْجَسَ مِنْهُمْ خِيفَةً﴾ [Hud: 70] (But when he saw that their hands did not reach it, he was suspicious of them and felt fear within himself). It was said: he disapproved of their greeting because it was not customary in their land. It was also said: he disapproved of their entering upon him without seeking permission.

﴿قَالُوا لَا تَوْجَلْ﴾ (They said, "Do not be fearful"): that is, the angels said, "Do not fear." It is also read as "lā tājal," and "lā tawjal" is from awjalahu, meaning: he frightened him. The clause ﴿إِنَّا نُبَشِّرُكَ بِغُلَامٍ عَلِيمٍ﴾ (Indeed, we give you good news of a knowing boy) is a new sentence giving the reason for the prohibition against fear. "ʿAlīm" means one of abundant knowledge. It was also said: it means "ḥalīm" (forbearing), as occurs in another place in the Qur'an. This boy is Isaac, as has preceded in Hud. He did not name him here, nor did he mention the good news of Jacob, being content with what had passed.

﴿قَالَ أَبَشَّرْتُمُونِي﴾ (He said, "Do you give me good news...?"): the majority read it with the interrogative alif (ʾabashshartumūnī). Al-Aʿmash read "bashshartumūnī" without the alif.

﴿عَلَىٰ أَن مَّسَّنِيَ الْكِبَرُ﴾ (...when old age has touched me): the clause is in the position of a circumstantial state, meaning: along with the state of old age and senility.

﴿فَبِمَ تُبَشِّرُونَ﴾ (Then by what will you give me good news?) is an interrogative of wonder, as if he was amazed at the child being born to him despite his having reached the decrepitude after which it is customary that no child is born. The meaning is: "By what thing do you give me good news? For good news of what is not customary is not valid."

Nafi' read ﴿تُبَشِّرُونِ﴾ (tubashshirūnī) with a kasra on the nūn and lightening (the shadda omitted), leaving the kasra to indicate the elided yāʾ.

Ibn Kathir and Ibn Muhaysin read it with a kasra on the nūn and a shadda, by assimilating the nūn into the nūn, its original form being tubashshirūnanī.

The rest read ﴿تُبَشِّرُونَ﴾ (tubashshirūna) with a fatḥa on the nūn.

﴿قَالُوا بَشَّرْنَاكَ بِالْحَقِّ﴾ (They said, "We have given you good news in truth"): that is, with certainty that admits no doubt, for that is the promise of God, and He does not fail in His promise, and nothing is impossible for Him, for He is capable of everything. ﴿فَلَا تَكُن مِّنَ الْقَانِطِينَ﴾ (So do not be among the despairing). The majority read it this way with the alif (al-qānitīn).

Al-Aʿmash and Yahya ibn Wathhab read ﴿مِنَ الْقَنِطِينَ﴾ (al-qanitīn) without the alif, and this is related from Abu ʿAmr, meaning: among those who despair of what We have given you good news of.

﴿قَالَ وَمَن يَقْنَطُ مِن رَّحْمَةِ رَبِّهِ إِلَّا الضَّالُّونَ﴾ (He said, "And who despairs of the mercy of his Lord except those astray?"): "yaqnaṭu" was read with a fatḥa on the nūn, and with a kasra, and both are dialects. A ḍamma on the nūn is also related. "Al-ḍāllūn" means those who deny, or those who err and stray from the path of correctness. That is: "I only found the child unlikely because of my old age, not because I despair of the mercy of my Lord."

Then he asked them about the reason God had sent them: ﴿قَالَ فَمَا خَطْبُكُمْ أَيُّهَا الْمُرْسَلُونَ﴾ (He said, "Then what is your business, O messengers?"). "Khaṭb" means a grave matter and a great affair. That is: what is your matter and your business, and what is it that you have come with other than what you have given me good news of? It seems he understood that their coming was not merely for the good news, but that they had another matter for which they were sent.

﴿قَالُوا إِنَّا أُرْسِلْنَا إِلَىٰ قَوْمٍ مُّجْرِمِينَ﴾ (They said, "Indeed, we have been sent to a wicked people"): that is, to a people who commit crimes, which includes association with God and what is lesser than it. These people are the people of Lot.

Then He excepted from them those who were not criminals, saying: ﴿إِلَّا آلَ لُوطٍ﴾ (except the family of Lot). This is a connected exception (istithnāʾ muttaṣil), because it is from the pronoun in "mujrimīn." Had it been from "qawm," it would have been a disconnected exception (munqaṭiʿ), since they had been described as criminals, and the family of Lot were not criminals. Then He mentioned what the family of Lot would be specially honored with, because they had not joined the people in their crimes, saying: ﴿إِنَّا لَمُنَجُّوهُمْ أَجْمَعِينَ﴾ (Indeed, We will surely save them all), that is, the family of Lot, who are his followers and the people of his religion. This clause is a new sentence on the assumption that the exception is connected, as if it was said: "What will be the state of the family of Lot?" So He said, "Indeed, We will surely save them all." But on the assumption that the exception is disconnected, it is a predicate (khabar), meaning: "But the family of Lot are saved from Our punishment."

Ḥamza and al-Kisa'i read ﴿لَمُنجُوهُمْ﴾ (lamunjūhum) with lightening, from anjā. The rest read it with the shadda, from najjā.

This last reading was chosen by Abu ʿUbayda and Abu Ḥatim. Tanjiyah and injā' both mean deliverance from what others have fallen into.

﴿إِلَّا امْرَأَتَهُ﴾ (except his wife): this exception is from the pronoun in "munjūhum," excluding her from those who are delivered, meaning: except his wife, who is not among those We deliver but among those We destroy. It was also said: the exception is from "the family of Lot" with respect to what was ruled for them of deliverance. The meaning is: they said, "Indeed, we have been sent to a wicked people to destroy them, except the family of Lot. Indeed, We will save them, except his wife, for she is among those who will be destroyed."

The meaning of ﴿قَدَّرْنَا إِنَّهَا لَمِنَ الْغَابِرِينَ﴾ (We have decreed that she will be among those who remain behind) is: We decided and judged that she is among those who remain in the punishment along with the disbelievers. "Al-ghābir" means the remaining one. The poet said:

*Do not sweep the she-camels of their remaining milk, for you do not know who will bear the young.*

"Al-ighbār" means the remnants of milk.

Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of "qaddarnā" is "we arranged," and it is close in meaning to "qaḍaynā" (we decreed). The original sense of taqdīr is making a thing to the measure of sufficiency.

ʿĀṣim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr and al-Mufaḍḍal, read "qadarnā" with lightening, and the rest read it with the shadda.

Al-Harawi said: the two have the same meaning. The decreeing was attributed to the angels, although it is an act of God, glorified is He, because of their nearness to God.

﴿فَلَمَّا جَاءَ آلَ لُوطٍ الْمُرْسَلُونَ﴾ (So when the messengers came to the family of Lot): this clause is a new sentence explaining the destruction of those who deserve destruction and the deliverance of those who deserve salvation.

﴿قَالَ إِنَّكُمْ قَوْمٌ مُّنكَرُونَ﴾ (He said, "Indeed, you are a people unknown [to me]"): that is, Lot said, addressing them, "Indeed, you are a people unknown," meaning: I do not know you, rather I disown you.

﴿قَالُوا بَلْ جِئْنَاكَ بِمَا كَانُوا فِيهِ يَمْتَرُونَ﴾ (They said, "Rather, we have brought you that about which they had been disputing"): that is, the punishment about which they had been doubting. So the turning away (iḍrāb) is from his claim that they had come with something he disowned. It is as if they said: "We have not come to you with what occurred to your mind of the hateful, rather we have come to you with what brings you joy, which is their punishment, which you warned them of, while they denied you."

﴿وَأَتَيْنَاكَ بِالْحَقِّ﴾ (And We have brought you the truth): that is, with certainty that admits no doubt or hesitation, which is the punishment descending upon them without fail. ﴿وَإِنَّا لَصَادِقُونَ﴾ (And indeed, We are truthful) in that report which We have informed you of.

The explanation of His saying ﴿فَأَسْرِ بِأَهْلِكَ بِقِطْعٍ مِّنَ اللَّيْلِ﴾ (So travel with your family during a part of the night) has already passed in surah Hud. ﴿وَاتَّبِعْ أَدْبَارَهُمْ﴾ (And follow behind them): that is, be behind them, driving them on, so that none of them lags behind and is struck by the punishment. ﴿وَلَا يَلْتَفِتْ مِنكُمْ أَحَدٌ﴾ (And let not one of you look back): that is, neither you nor any of them should turn around and see what punishment has befallen them, lest he become occupied with looking at it, and slow down from the swiftness of the journey and from distancing himself from the abodes of the wrongdoers. It was also said: the meaning of "lā yaltafit" is "lā yatakhalladh" (let no one fall behind). ﴿وَامْضُوا حَيْثُ تُؤْمَرُونَ﴾ (And proceed to where you are commanded): that is, to the direction in which God, glorified is He, commanded you to proceed, which is the direction of the Levant (al-Sham). It was also said: Egypt; it was also said: a village of the villages of Lot; and it was also said: the land of the Friend (al-Khalil, Abraham).

﴿وَقَضَيْنَا إِلَيْهِ﴾ (And We conveyed to him): that is, We revealed to Lot ﴿ذَلِكَ الْأَمْرَ﴾ (that matter), which is the destruction of his people. Then He explained it with His saying: ﴿أَنَّ دَابِرَ هَٰؤُلَاءِ مَقْطُوعٌ مُّصْبِحِينَ﴾ (that the last of these people would be cut off at daybreak). Al-Zajjaj said: the position of "anna" is accusative, and it is a substitute (badal) for ﴿ذَلِكَ الْأَمْرَ﴾. "Al-dābir" is the last one, meaning: the last of them who remains will be destroyed at the time of morning. The accusative of "muṣbiḥīn" is a circumstantial state, meaning: while they are entering upon the time of morning. A similar expression is His saying: ﴿فَقُطِعَ دَابِرُ الْقَوْمِ الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا﴾ [al-An'am: 45] (So the last of the people who did wrong was cut off).

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Dahhak, regarding His saying "āminīn" (secure), that he said: they were secure from death, so they do not die, nor do they grow old, nor do they fall ill, nor do they become naked, nor do they become hungry.

Ibn Jarir related from ʿAlī regarding ﴿وَنَزَعْنَا مَا فِي صُدُورِهِم مِّنْ غِلٍّ﴾ that he said: "It is enmity."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Mardawayh related from al-Hasan al-Basri that he said: ʿAlī ibn Abi Talib said: "By God, it was about us that the people of Paradise were revealed: ﴿وَنَزَعْنَا مَا فِي صُدُورِهِم مِّنْ غِلٍّ إِخْوَانًا عَلَىٰ سُرُرٍ مُّتَقَابِلِينَ﴾ (And We will remove whatever resentment is in their breasts, as brothers, on couches facing one another)."

Ibn 'Asakir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him concerning this verse, saying: It was revealed concerning three Arab tribes: Banu Hashim, Banu Taym, and Banu 'Adi, concerning me and Abu Bakr and 'Umar.

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn 'Asakir narrated from Kathir al-Nawwa', who said: I said to Abu Ja'far, "So-and-so narrated to me from 'Ali ibn al-Husayn that this verse was revealed concerning Abu Bakr, 'Umar, and 'Ali: ﴿And We removed whatever resentment was in their breasts﴾." He said: "By Allah, it was indeed revealed concerning them. And concerning whom else would it be revealed, if not them?" I said: "And what is this resentment?" He said: "It is the resentment of the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period of ignorance). Banu Taym, Banu 'Adi, and Banu Hashim had enmity between them in the Jahiliyyah. When these people embraced Islam, they loved one another. Then Abu Bakr was seized by a pain in his side, so 'Ali began to warm his hand and rub it on Abu Bakr's side, and this verse was revealed."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'Ali, through several chains, that he said to Ibn Talhah: "I hope that I and your father will be among those concerning whom Allah said: ﴿And We removed whatever resentment was in their breasts﴾, the verse." A man from Hamdan said: "Allah is more just than that." 'Ali cried out at him with a cry by which the palace shook, and said: "Then who, if we are not those?"

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'Ali that he said: "I hope that I, 'Uthman, al-Zubayr, and Talhah will be among those concerning whom Allah said: ﴿And We removed whatever resentment was in their breasts﴾."

Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn 'Asakir narrated through the route of al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning this verse, that he said: It was revealed concerning ten: Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Uthman, 'Ali, Talhah, al-Zubayr, Sa'd, Sa'id, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf, and 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud.
